articles.title_orig: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
articles.title_zh: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
articles.content_orig:
China has rejected allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".
US intelligence officials believe that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, was gathering information for Beijing on the US chip-making giant, according to a report by The New York Times .
The report said Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was under investigation over the possible diversion of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China and had developed a close relationship with Jensen.
Nvidia told the paper their interactions were routine business engagements, while Beijing accused Washington of attempting to smear China. Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.
The BBC has contacted Nvidia and Megaspeed for comment.
US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.
Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".
It remains unclear what information Alice Huang - who is also known as Huang Le - allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.
At a regular briefing on Friday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said: "The report in question is based on groundless speculation and is nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
The paper's report comes amid longstanding US concerns about China's access to advanced computing technology, which is considered crucial to developing artificial intelligence systems.
Jensen Huang has argued that allowing Nvidia to sell more of its products to China is important for maintaining US competitiveness in the global AI industry.
But Washington has restricted exports of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022, citing national security concerns and the risk that the technology could strengthen China's military operations. There have however been some loosening of restrictions during Trump's administration.
US officials said they had caught several firms illegally trafficking the chips across the Chinese border. They have also investigated whether companies operating through third countries are helping Chinese businesses access the restricted technology.
Nvidia has said it complies with applicable export laws and that there is no evidence its chips have been smuggled into China.
In response to the allegations made by the Times, John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, told the paper: "Jensen's interactions with Ms Huang are not unusual or unexpected".
He said customers like Megaspeed "receive ordinary business information - not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets - and zero information relevant to national security."
He added that allegations the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China "were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year".
Megaspeed said its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. The company also said it had informed the US government that it was willing to cooperate.
It is unclear how closely Alice Huang remains involved with Megaspeed.

articles.title_orig: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report
articles.title_zh: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report
articles.content_orig:
IISS study questions overreliance on American support and ‘overdependence on expensive, high-end systems’
Gulf states are going to have to reconfigure their trillion-dollar defences given the damage inflicted on their economies and the questionable continued value of US bases in the face of Iranian attack, according to a study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
The report says that in the weeks before the 8 April ceasefire, 12 regional states, overwhelmingly in the Gulf, faced 4,670 Iranian one-way attack drones and more than 1,400 ballistic missiles. Nearly half were aimed at the United Arab Emirates . Although the vast majority were repelled, one estimate of the damage to energy infrastructure cited by the report is put as high as $58bn (£43bn).
Iran would portray either a reduction or complete withdrawal of US forces from the region as “a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness, but also use it to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection”.
The report says the war also highlights another “uncomfortable truth for the Gulf states: not only has their trillion-dollar acquisition of US weapons not translated into US protection at the crucial time, but their respective militaries are also not adequately prepared for the new kind of attritional air war to which they are being exposed”.
Despite huge investment in mainly US armaments, the report identified significant shortcomings: “overwhelming reliance on US-supplied air- and missile-defence systems and munitions; a failure to achieve regional defence integration; a shortage of minesweeping capability; limited retaliatory options; and the prohibitive costs stemming from an overdependence on expensive, high-end systems to take down relatively inexpensive drones and missiles”.
The report is neutral on whether the divided Gulf states should seek a new non-aggression pact with Iran, but notes that the US-Iran war has shown longstanding defence and security partnerships with the US “have failed to ensure adequate protection against Iranian aggression”.
It adds: “If anything, US military bases and defence partnerships with the US have provided Iran with another pretext for attacks against the Gulf states.”
Public opinion on the US in the Gulf has also been shifting, it says, “from security provider to strategic liability”.
Any reduction or withdrawal of US forces from the Gulf region would be portrayed by Iran “as a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness” and would also be used “to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection,” the report notes.
after newsletter promotion
The study comes after Chris Murphy, the Democrat senator and member of the senate foreign relations committee, said a debate was under way in the US military about the value of seeking to rebuild the damaged US bases in the Gulf.
Murphy said the Gulf state leadership “want us to rebuild” and “to keep a presence in the region”, but asked: “What good is it to have a base in the region to protect American interests if within 24 hours of a hot war starting, it is wiped off the map?
“We would be criminally incompetent as stewards of taxpayer dollars if we were to rebuild bases that are blown up within hours of the next war starting.
“So clearly, we are going to have to have a smaller footprint in the region, and the limiting principle on the footprint that we rebuild will be ‘what can we protect?’ because we clearly cannot protect the scope of our footprint today and if we can’t protect it, it is useless.”
Murphy suggested that, at the very least, the US may need to relocate its bases in the eastern Mediterranean further away from Iranian missiles.

articles.title_orig: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew and Epstein Balmoral visits
articles.title_zh: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew and Epstein Balmoral visits
articles.content_orig:
Police Scotland is making inquiries into the activities of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell during their time at Balmoral Castle.
The Daily Express reported that the inquiry relates to allegations that women were trafficked to the royal residence in Aberdeenshire.
Sex offender Epstein - who died in 2019 - and Maxwell, who was jailed in 2022 for sex trafficking , are understood to have visited the castle with Mountbatten-Windsor, who has previously denied any wrongdoing.
Police Scotland said inquiries were at "a very early stage" and that it would be inappropriate to comment further.
Representatives of Mountbatten-Windsor have been contacted for comment.
The Royal family traditionally spend summer at Balmoral, where Queen Elizabeth II died in 2022.
Asked about the Express report, a Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We have received information and active inquiries are ongoing but these are at a very early stage.
"All inquiries are evidence led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries.
"We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further."
In February, the force said it wanted to "speak to anyone with information" about Epstein's private jet using Edinburgh Airport.
At the time officers said they had not received any reports or complaints in relating to the trip.
Flight logs show Mountbatten-Windsor and Maxwell flew from Luton to Edinburgh on Epstein's private jet with two other passengers on 1 September 2006.
An image believed to show disgraced financier Epstein and former socialite Maxwell at Balmoral was also released by US prosecutors during her sex trafficking trial.
It is thought to have been taken in 1999, when Mountbatten-Windsor reportedly invited the couple to stay at the castle.
Epstein and Maxwell were reportedly regular guests at royal residences in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Last year, the so-called Epstein Files were released by the US Department of Justice.
Among them was an email from someone named 'A' to Maxwell which said they were at Balmoral and asked for "new inappropriate friends".
The message, sent to Maxwell on 16 August 2001, begins: "I am up here at Balmoral Summer Camp for the Royal Family."
Later in the email, the sender asks: "How's LA? Have you found me some new inappropriate friends?" before signing off "see ya A xxx".
Jeffrey Epstein was 66 when he died by suicide in 2019 in a US prison while awaiting trial for sex trafficking charges.
Maxwell, 60, was jailed for 20 years in 2022 for her role in procuring girls for Epstein.
Last October it was confirmed Andrew had been stripped of his "prince" title and would be leaving his Windsor mansion, Royal Lodge.
In February he was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office , in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the US, and later released.
Earlier this month it emerged he was taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over search warrants issued before his arrest.
Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein.

articles.title_orig: ‘It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is’: Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson on Europe's incumbency problem
articles.title_zh: ‘It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is’: Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson on Europe's incumbency problem
articles.content_orig:
The brutal business of selling mirrors is not for the faint-hearted. The challenge is category differentiation, given that a mirror has one simple task—reflection. One of Greg Jackson’s first jobs was working for a mirror manufacturer which, at best, broke even or made a small profit. And then he had an idea.
“We started making mirrors that had really wide frames,” the founder of Octopus Energy (the U.K.’s largest energy provider) told me. “And on a picture [on the internet], suddenly we had a mirror that looked different from everybody else’s. And they sold like hotcakes – and that transformed the business.”
Approaching a business from a different point of view is an essential ingredient in the hunt for innovation. Jackson’s essential insight when it came to mirrors was that, online, every product looked the same. That is what the customer saw. And he realized that if the customer saw something different (a mirror with a wide frame), they might buy it. Which they did.
Not seeing something that is obvious to an outsider is a firm’s “incumbency cost”— embedded in the regular behavior of doing the same thing tomorrow as you did yesterday. It is one of the most significant brakes on the ability to grow.
“I think the single biggest factor affecting Europe—and an issue the U.S. is not immune to—is incumbency,” he told me. “China and the Gulf are not held back by incumbent industries. Instead they are, at huge pace, delivering the new world. If I look at electric vehicles as an example, there’s not an incumbent car industry in China that’s struggling to manage the transition to an entirely new technology. But if I look at Europe, European governments and consumers want electric vehicles, but the European car companies have not yet been able to be competitive at building them.”
“If we want more growth, we need to allow creative destruction so new companies can deliver the productivity we need”
Chinese electric vehicle sales in Europe are growing rapidly. Chery has tripled sales in Europe in the past year, BYD has doubled, Geely is up a third, and SAIC is up 23%. Taking the four leading Chinese car makers together, their EV market share is now at 14.6%, up from 9.6%, according to the latest figures from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association. In response to claims of state subsidized dumping by China, the European Union has applied duties of up to 35% on top of the standard 10% import tariff. Chinese cars are still over 20% cheaper to buy.
“Incumbents crowd out the innovators in many sectors and markets,” Jackson said. “It wasn’t the Post Office [the U.K.’s public mail service] that invented email. The music industry held back streaming and digital music for 10 to 20 years. What you need is routes to market for new technologies, and I think that can be a challenge in Europe because so many of the big industries essentially have a stranglehold on policy.
“Economists have said that nearly all productivity growth comes from new companies. If we want more growth, we need to allow creative destruction so new companies can deliver the productivity we need.”
Jackson said that Europe has a number of successful sectors that it can learn from—for example, the continent enjoys a vibrant and innovative fintech sector whereas in America “they take my card around the back of the bar because their terminals and processes are so dated.” Few people have seen a check in Europe in more than a decade.
Octopus grew out of the need for a new way to manage energy supply and demand. Jackson initially attempted to convince legacy businesses that they would be far more efficient with a fully overhauled technology platform but, after not progressing very far, decided that he could build a team that could modernize more quickly.
“The idea was that through technology, we would be able to provide lower costs because we’d be more operationally efficient,” he said. “We’d be more agile, so we can incorporate technologies like electric vehicles and solar panels and batteries directly into the energy system very efficiently. That would also help with cleaning up energy because you can use more renewables more cost-effectively if you’re more agile. We set out building that company in 2015, and nine years later, we became the biggest energy company in the UK, overtaking all the incumbents.
“We came from outside energy, we came from tech, and just like the people that built Uber didn’t come from personal transportation, and the people that built Airbnb didn’t come from hospitality, and the people that built Amazon didn’t own bookshops. What we were able to do is build an energy company not based around the assumptions of the industry, but using technology to meet the needs of customers.”
The brute force of market dynamics is pushing the world towards a different energy mix. In the European Union, wind and solar power produced more electricity than fossil fuels for the first time last year, according to Ember, the energy think tank.
“The technologies of electricity are improving exponentially, and the technologies of hydrocarbons are not,” Jackson said. “A car engine costs roughly the same now as it did 20 years ago. They’re not particularly more efficient. Meanwhile, an electric vehicle battery today costs 10 times less than it did 15 years ago. Solar panels cost 200 times less than they did 40 years ago. Wind turbines have come down two thirds in price over the last 20 years.”
Jackson was in China earlier in the year and said that electrification is continuing at pace, with battery swap stations, rather than recharging, reducing the amount of time drivers have to wait to between three and five minutes. “It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is. The drivers don’t care about the price of diesel.” Which might give Donald Trump pause for thought as he eyes both the American mid-term elections and the rising cost of fuel in the U.S.

Training off Second Thomas and Sabina shoals tests small boats, surveillance drones and simulated vessel boardings amid ongoing spats
China’s coastguard has carried out an exercise featuring water cannons and drones near two disputed reefs at the centre of its simmering South China Sea contention with the Philippines to prepare for “foreign infringement”, according to state media.
A China Coast Guard flotilla “recently” conducted “comprehensive maritime law-enforcement training” in the waters around Second Thomas Shoal and Sabina Shoal, according to state broadcaster CCTV, which did not specify dates.
The official television network stated that the drill had focused on foreign vessels “illegally” entering the waters around the two shoals, while covering surveillance, tracking, maritime traffic control and tactical manoeuvres by small boats.
It also included practising water cannon use, drone operations and optoelectronic evidence collection – a technique that uses optical and electronic sensors to detect and record evidence that may not be visible to the naked eye – according to the report.

articles.title_orig: Footage of Seoul crush to be removed from Call of Duty after backlash
articles.title_zh: Footage of Seoul crush to be removed from Call of Duty after backlash
articles.content_orig:
Video clips showing the aftermath of a deadly crush in Seoul will be removed from the latest Call of Duty game after an angry reaction from victims' families.
Real life news coverage of the 2022 disaster which killed almost 160 people was included in an opening scene of Modern Warfare 4 to illustrate a fictional invasion from North Korea.
Bereaved families said they were "appalled" to see the footage - which included people being removed on stretchers, body bags on the street and resuscitation efforts - repurposed for the game.
Activision, which makes Call of Duty, has since apologised and confirmed it would be removed in the game's next update on 12 November.
The crush happened in the narrow alleys of Seoul's Itaewon district when more than 100,000 people went to the area to celebrate Halloween four years ago.
The streets became so tightly packed that people could not move and some were unable to breathe.
In a statement on Thursday , the families of those who died said the disaster "was a tragedy that caused hundreds of casualties, and citizens who took part in the rescue or witnessed it have suffered from trauma until now".
"We cannot help but be appalled that the chaotic and desperate scene, in which many citizens at the site performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the freezing street, was used to create a scene in a game.
"Using such an event as material for a game made for entertainment is in itself highly inappropriate and senseless."
Activision confirmed it had used real news coverage of the disaster "to establish the game's fictional narrative" but insisted it had "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form".
Confirming on Friday that the footage would be removed in a statement, the company offered its condolences and apologised to the bereaved families and victims who have been hurt by this incident.
The decision was welcomed by the 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association, however the group told the BBC they had not received a direct apology from Activision.
Modern Warfare 4, which was released last week, had already faced criticism for basing the game on North Korea invading South Korea, as the two countries have been technically at war for decades.
Fighting stopped in the Korean War in 1953, but the two countries never signed a peace treaty and conflict is a very real worry in that part of the world.
At the launch of the game, Call of Duty's chief marketing officer, Tyler Bahl, told BBC Newsbeat: "We have to understand this is entertainment".

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's relationship with China just got even more complicated as report says Jensen Huang was target of spy plot
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's relationship with China just got even more complicated as report says Jensen Huang was target of spy plot
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) business is booming, but one sector of the market remains a seemingly impenetrable morass for the world's leading chip designer: China.
For years, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has struggled to gain a foothold in the world's second-largest economy, due in large part to restrictions imposed by the Department of Commerce, which regulates international chip sales. Seeking inroads, Huang has repeatedly urged the White House to loosen those restrictions, which the administration says are necessary for national security and for the US to remain ahead in the AI race.
When Nvidia last reported earnings, forward guidance once again omitted sales projections for China, continually snarled by state politics.
Nvidia stock fell 3% before the bell on Friday.
The complicated relationship between Nvidia and China was thrust back into public light on Thursday after the New York Times reported new US intelligence efforts. The US intelligence service, the report says, believes a Chinese national named Alice Huang — who has served as a leader of Nvidia chip customer Megaspeed and who maintains a well-documented relationship with Huang himself — has acted as an intelligence asset and passed information to the governing party in Beijing.
The reporting raises major questions about potential information leakage from Nvidia to China, not only regarding trade secrets but also about Jensen Huang's increasingly deep ties to the White House as he has lobbied for eased restrictions. At the All-In summit in September, Huang took a call from Trump on stage, putting the US leader on speakerphone as Trump dismissed fears around AI's security implications as a "scam."
The race between the US and China to develop and disseminate their own AI technology has, over the past several years, become a paramount concern for the leadership of both governments.
While China has matched or even surpassed the US on the development and distribution of "open weight" AI models, which often come at far cheaper costs than "closed weight" alternatives, the US frontier labs such as Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) and OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) have retained the lead in developing the most advanced models.
Powering those advanced models are chips designed by Nvidia, whose leading semiconductors are often regarded as the gold standard for computing performance. While the chips are hugely popular in the US and other global markets, the Commerce Department has, since 2022, blocked Nvidia from selling successive generations of its chips to Chinese buyers as Washington seeks to maintain its edge over Beijing.
Huang won a victory for his company in December 2025 when he secured permission from the Trump administration for Nvidia to export some H200 chips to Chinese buyers, a policy change that came amid a $5 million lobbying push by Nvidia throughout the year. Even chip models such as the H200, which are now several generations behind Nvidia's flagship products, remain competitive for Chinese buyers with options available from companies like Huawei Technologies.
Yet H200 sales accounted for less than 1% of Nvidia's $89 billion in data center revenue for the second quarter, Nvidia said. Part of that dearth in sales has also come from Beijing, which recently moved to block Chinese buyers from purchasing Nvidia chips as Xi Jinping's government looks to reduce dependence on US technology, instead turning to homegrown alternatives from the likes of Huawei.
Given the "ongoing geopolitical uncertainty," Nvidia CFO Colette Kress told analysts, "there is no China data center compute revenue in our forward outlook."
While it's not clear how many H200 chips Nvidia sold to Chinese buyers in the second quarter, those sales fell below the US-approved maximum due to blocks imposed by the Chinese government, the company said.
"Under the current rules and geopolitical landscape, we are unable to create and deliver a competitive product for wide distribution in China's data center market with the approval from both the USG and the Chinese government," Nvidia said in its second quarter earnings report.
The restrictions haven't stopped Chinese buyers from pursuing workarounds to obtain some of the world's leading chips.
Since the US government imposed its sales restrictions on Nvidia, a black-market shadow trade has sprung up in response, according to public reporting and investigations by the Department of Justice . Buyers and sellers throughout Southeast Asian nations not under restrictions import chips under legitimate guises, then switch labels , change packaging, or use other methods to disguise the package's true contents before sending the chips onward into China, reporting and the US government have alleged.
Inside China, users on Douyin, the nation's version of TikTok, openly hawk sanctioned chips such as Nvidia's Blackwell B300, priced at millions of US dollars per server, in videos reviewed by Yahoo Finance. Such sales would likely contravene the Commerce Department's restrictions.
Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company that employed Alice Huang, has been investigated by US authorities for more than a year due to concerns that the company may be sending Nvidia's most advanced chips to data centers throughout Southeast Asia that serve Chinese companies or directly funneling the physical chips into China through intermediaries, per the New York Times.
Nvidia has repeatedly stated that there's no evidence its chips are being smuggled into China, and the company said to the New York Times that if someone close to the company were a "threat to American industry," Nvidia is confident the US government would make the company aware. The company added that while Huang often talks with customers, those conversations never include "information relevant to national security."
Even so, for Huang and Nvidia, the headlines come as a reminder of the geopolitical tensions inherent to the AI trade.
While it's in Nvidia's interest to serve as wide a customer base as possible, national security concerns in Washington continue to interfere with the company's ability to sell into the world's second-largest economy, where buyers have shown willingness to pay top dollar for its products.
Correction: A previous version of this story misstated where Huang took a call from Trump on stage. It was at the All-In Summit.

articles.title_orig: Aliyev's snub of Turkic summit brings Azerbaijan-Turkey tensions to fore
articles.title_zh: Aliyev's snub of Turkic summit brings Azerbaijan-Turkey tensions to fore
articles.content_orig:
Türkiye and Uzbekistan signed five agreements on Thursday aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation in trade, social security and business development following a meeting between President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in Ankara.
The agreements were signed at the Presidential Complex after Erdoğan held talks with Mirziyoyev, who arrived in the Turkish capital to attend the 13th Organization of Turkic States (OTS) summit.
Erdoğan invited Mirziyoyev to the COP31 Leaders Summit in Antalya during talks in Ankara focused on strengthening bilateral ties and expanding cooperation among Turkic states.
He reaffirmed Ankara's commitment to deepening its high-level strategic partnership with Tashkent, particularly in trade, investment, mining, transportation and the defense industry.
He also expressed confidence that the OTS would continue to grow stronger through new cooperation initiatives, voicing hope that the upcoming leaders' summit in Ankara would mark a significant milestone for the organization.
Erdoğan welcomed his Uzbek counterpart at the entrance of the Presidential Complex before their meeting.
The agreements included an additional protocol amending a 2022 arrangement on the advance exchange of information concerning vehicles and goods crossing national borders, signed by Turkish Trade Minister Ömer Bolat and Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov.
A separate protocol amending the preferential trade agreement between the two countries was signed by Bolat and Uzbek Minister of Investment, Industry and Trade Laziz Kudratov.
Turkish Labor and Social Security Minister Vedat Işıkhan and Saidov signed a bilateral social security agreement, along with a separate administrative agreement governing its implementation.
Erdoğan and Mirziyoyev also signed an agreement establishing a high-level council to support the business community and strengthen economic cooperation between the two countries.
The agreements come as Ankara and Tashkent seek to expand bilateral trade, which reached $3.1 billion in 2025, toward their shared target of $5 billion.
Earlier Thursday, Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz welcomed Mirziyoyev, Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov and Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov at the airport ahead of the OTS summit.
In a statement shared on the Turkish social media platform NSosyal, Yılmaz expressed hope that the gathering would strengthen solidarity and cooperation among Turkic states.

articles.title_orig: Russia ‘forces’ closure of investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta
articles.title_zh: Russia ‘forces’ closure of investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta
articles.content_orig:
Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced it will shut down, citing pressure from the authorities.
The independent outlet’s editorial board said in a statement released on Friday that the newspaper has been forced to end its operations.
The Russian media has come under increased scrutiny from the state amid Moscow’s war on Ukraine. The authorities recently searched the home of Novaya Gazeta’s senior editor and arrested the editor-in-chief.
“The newspaper is gone. The Russian authorities and … intelligence services forced the editorial staff to cease operations,” the editorial board said in the statement , which was entitled: “We were killed.”
Viewed as a relative bastion of independent journalism in Russia, Novaya Gazeta has been classed as a “foreign agent” by Moscow, a label used to stifle dissent.
“Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist,” editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov said in a video statement published on YouTube. “On November 9 we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave.”
Earlier this month, Sokolov was taken in for questioning as Russian authorities searched his home due, they said, to a link to a criminal case involving his colleague Oleg Roldugin.
Roldugin was arrested in April and charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”.
“How far will the Kremlin’s relentless campaign against Novaya Gazeta go?” asked media watchdog Reporters Without Borders in a statement after Sokolov was arrested on October 15.
“Six of its journalists and staff members have been murdered, its newsroom has been raided, its journalists have been prosecuted, and the publication has been designated a ‘foreign agent’,” the press freedom organisation noted.
The forced closure of Novaya Gazeta marks another escalation in Russia’s crackdown on press freedom, with few independent media outlets or journalists left in the country, as censorship levels and arrests of regime critics have skyrocketed since it launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The newspaper had already trimmed production inside Russia after Moscow invaded Ukraine, as authorities revoked its media licence.
The paper’s then editor-in-chief, Dmitry Muratov, jointly won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 for his “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression” at the helm of the paper.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu’s bloc loses parliamentary majority, Justice Department subpoenas California officials
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu’s bloc loses parliamentary majority, Justice Department subpoenas California officials
articles.content_orig:
As coalition negotiations loom and allegations of foreign election interference emerge, Fox News Digital reporter Efrat Lachter reports from Tel Aviv, Israel.
Israel's final election count has confirmed that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc has lost its parliamentary majority, but whether opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot can assemble a government to replace him remains an open question as negotiations begin behind closed doors.
The completed count, published early Friday by Israel's Central Elections Committee , gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for Eisenkot's opposition alliance. The two predominantly Arab parties secured a historic 19 seats, placing them in a potentially decisive position.
Netanyahu's Likud emerged as the largest individual party with 27 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar with 21 and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett's Beyachad with 12. Final voter turnout reached 77.9%, according to the Central Elections Committee results .
ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW
Posters of former Israeli Chief of General Staff and Yashar Party leader Gadi Eisenkot, right, and Prime Minister and Likud Party leader Benjamin Netanyahu are seen as election campaigns intensify two days before the vote as campaign posters of candidates are displayed on billboards and buildings across the streets ahead of the Knesset elections scheduled for October 27, in Tel Aviv, Israel, on October 25, 2026. (Nir Keidar/Anadolu via Getty Images)
But the numbers leave neither major bloc with the 61 seats required for a majority, opening a complex political struggle involving potential partnerships with Arab parties, ultra-Orthodox lawmakers or a unity government bringing together longtime rivals.
A source familiar with opposition discussions, who spoke to Fox News Digital on condition of anonymity, described the outcome as a "bitter stalemate," but not an impossible political situation.
The source said opposition leaders are approaching coalition negotiations with patience and experience rather than treating the inconclusive results as a defeat, arguing that the next government could depend on their ability to forge partnerships that previously seemed unlikely.
FORMER ISRAELI ARMY CHIEF GADI EISENKOT EMERGES AS NETANYAHU’S LEADING ELECTION CHALLENGER
An ultra-Orthodox Jewish man holds his ballot as he votes in the parliamentary election at a polling station in Jerusalem on January 22, 2013. Israelis voted on Tuesday in an election widely expected to win Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a third term in office, pushing the Jewish State further to the right, away from peace with Palestinians and towards a showdown with Iran. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)
In a potentially significant development Friday, Israeli journalist Yishai Cohen of Kikar HaShabbat reported that Rabbi Dov Lando, a leading ultra-Orthodox religious authority, had instructed lawmakers from Degel HaTorah, part of United Torah Judaism, to open discussions with the opposition.
According to the report, the objective is to reach an arrangement protecting the status of yeshiva students amid the longstanding dispute over mandatory military service.
Channel 12 reported that figures within the ultra-Orthodox party were considering allowing an Eisenkot-led minority government to survive through outside parliamentary support, potentially breaking with Netanyahu.
"Our votes are not in Netanyahu's pocket," party figures told Channel 12, according to a translation of the Hebrew-language report.
However, the office of United Torah Judaism Chairman Yaakov Asher denied that any instruction to begin negotiations had been issued.
Such an arrangement would represent a significant shift from the party's longstanding alliance with Netanyahu. Eisenkot's pledge to expand military conscription among ultra-Orthodox men remains a major obstacle, although Channel 12 reported that party figures were willing to consider a compromise on the issue.
The source familiar with opposition discussions told Fox News Digital that Eisenkot's camp had been preparing for the possibility of cooperation with ultra-Orthodox parties well before the election, suggesting that some of the options now being discussed had already been under consideration behind the scenes.
According to the source, such an arrangement could require compromises over military service and potentially outside parliamentary support from Arab lawmakers, bringing together political factions whose positions appeared irreconcilable during the campaign.
FORMER ISRAELI PM EMERGES AS WILD CARD IN HIGH-STAKES ELECTION WITH MIDDLE EAST'S FUTURE AT STAKE
People gather near a pre-election campaign banner featuring leaders of the Joint List, ahead of Israel's national election, in Nazareth, Israel, on October 10, 2026. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)
Another possibility rests with the Arab parties, which nearly doubled their parliamentary representation from 10 to 19 seats following a surge in turnout.
But the prospects of an Arab-backed government have drawn conflicting assessments.
Channel 12 reported Thursday that Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas had expressed deep skepticism about the possibility of establishing an Eisenkot-led minority government supported by Arab lawmakers.
Israeli political commentator Amit Segal also argued that the available options had narrowed considerably, identifying a Netanyahu-Eisenkot unity government or another election as the two principal remaining possibilities.
Mohammed Majadla, head of the news division at Radio Nas and a Channel 12 political commentator, offered a different assessment in an interview with Fox News Digital, arguing that both Ra'am and the Joint List were prepared to use their parliamentary influence to prevent Netanyahu from returning to power.
"The two Arab lists agree on two things," Majadla said in the Hebrew-language interview. "First, they are prepared to do everything within the political process to ensure Netanyahu does not return to power."
According to Majadla, that could include joining a coalition, providing outside parliamentary support or abstaining from key votes.
He said their second shared priority was avoiding another election, which Arab political leaders fear could reverse their gains.
"The ball is now in Eisenkot's court, not in the Arab parties' court," Majadla said. "As far as the Arab parties are concerned, I can tell you they are truly prepared to do everything to make this happen."
Majadla suggested that public declarations should not necessarily be treated as final positions, particularly as parties seek leverage during coalition negotiations.
The difficulties extend beyond the Arab parties. Eisenkot's potential partners include politicians who strongly oppose cooperation with ultra-Orthodox factions, while several opposition leaders campaigned against relying on Arab lawmakers to govern.
NETANYAHU FIGHTS FOR POLITICAL FUTURE AS ISRAEL HEADS TO POLLS WITH IRAN THREAT LOOMING
A road sign stands in front of a large billboard featuring Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, of the Likud Party and former military chief and leader of the centrist Yashar Party, Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan on October 20, 2026. Israel heads to the polls on October 27 in its first election since the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, in what is seen as a referendum on the prime minister. (Jack Guez / AFP via Getty Images)
A national unity government involving Likud and Yashar would offer a more straightforward mathematical route to a majority, but would require Eisenkot to reconsider his campaign pledge not to join a Netanyahu-led government.
For Netanyahu, the lengthy coalition formation process could provide additional opportunities. If Eisenkot receives the mandate to form a government but fails, President Isaac Herzog could assign the task to another candidate, potentially giving Netanyahu another chance to assemble a coalition. articles.title_orig: Pentagon tells Europeans to cool their rhetoric on Russia, sources say
articles.title_zh: Pentagon tells Europeans to cool their rhetoric on Russia, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Antoni Slodkowski, Gram Slattery and Andrius Sytas, Reuters
Pentagon officials have in recent weeks asked several NATO countries to tone down their rhetoric regarding the threat posed by Russia, arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials have undermined continental security, four people familiar with the matter said.
Among the nations that have received messages urging them to keep public statements in check are Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity. It was not clear if the messages, which were delivered in bilateral meetings, were conveyed to other European governments.
The U.S. requests come as the Trump administration restarts an effort to press for a negotiated end to the full-scale war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year. The latest push has blended incentives for Russia – including sanctions relief – with pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Asked for comment, a Pentagon official said: “Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations.”
Among the comments that have drawn U.S. officials’ attention are suggestions by European leaders that Russia is cornered and resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine slows to a crawl, one of the people said.
Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, a key figure in an ongoing review of U.S. troop levels in Europe, was one of the U.S. officials delivering the message, the people said. Reuters could not determine what other officials were involved.
None of the people, who include three European officials and a U.S. official, suggested the advice was communicated in a confrontational manner.
The U.S. messages reflect a debate within NATO regarding how to publicly address the threat of an increasingly assertive Russia.
Some Western officials have argued that emphasizing the threat posed by Moscow could play into the hands of the Kremlin, which they say seeks to sow fear and undermine support for Ukraine.
Others argue European governments must be transparent to show their electorates that sacrifice and resources are needed to keep Moscow at bay. That is especially true as Russia appears to accelerate a covert campaign of sabotage throughout the continent.
Russia has denied that it is pursuing such a campaign.
One of the people familiar told Reuters that Colby told a Baltic official recently that there should be no “poking” directed at the Russians.
The person said Colby pointed to Europeans publicly suggesting that Russia was “cornered like a rat” as an example of unhelpful rhetoric.
It was not clear what specific statement Colby was referring to. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal referred to Putin as a “rat in a corner” in late September, suggesting the Russian leader was resorting to sabotage efforts in Europe as Russia had become increasingly bogged down in Ukraine.
“We are helping you. The Americans are there,” said a separate European official, describing the Pentagon’s recent private messaging. “Just don’t be loud. Don’t make noise.”
In a separate recent meeting, the Pentagon urged an Estonian delegation to be “measured” in its communications, according to a person briefed on the encounter, though the person did not say Pentagon officials complained about any specific statement.
The defense ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to requests for comment, while NATO declined to comment.
One of the European officials said that the Pentagon’s advice, while cordial, was baffling, given that intelligence services in the Baltic states have in recent months consistently played down the probability of Russia testing NATO’s mutual defense provisions.
Other NATO intelligence services, by contrast, have publicly warned that Russia could dramatically ramp up its sabotage campaign in the near future.
The Pentagon messages to NATO officials come at a fraught time for European security.
Moscow has recently intensified its campaign of deniable attacks on NATO countries, Western intelligence officials have said.
On Wednesday, German prosecutors said two Belarusians were arrested for allegedly planning to set fire to a building or critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg area. In September, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, allegations Moscow has denied.
At the same time, U.S. officials have been discussing potential business deals with Russia as part of the Trump administration’s push for peace in Ukraine. Those efforts have drawn mixed reactions from European officials, many of whom are pushing for the Kremlin’s continued economic isolation.
Pentagon planners, meanwhile, are reviewing Washington’s force posture in Europe, a process that could see a sharp drawdown in America’s troop presence on the continent.
US officials have said European NATO members need to assume more responsibility for their own defense, particularly as the US focuses on threats in the Middle East, Latin America and East Asia.
Antoni Slodkowski, Gram Slattery and Andrius Sytas, Reuters

articles.title_orig: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
articles.title_zh: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
articles.content_orig:
Strikes are planned across Italy on Friday, with widespread disruption expected as trade union Unione Sindacale di Base called on both public and private sector workers to strike, mobilise and protest, including at a major demonstration in Rome.
Renewed student protests are also expected to return to the street in major cities across Italy.
Meanwhile, the Cobas unions, together with Adl, Clap and Sial, have also called for a general strike across the public and private sectors, excluding transport.
The strike will also be a new test for public order, as students are set to return to the streets in all the main cities across Italy.
Friday's protests are directed against the rising cost of living, which unions say makes it increasingly difficult for people to cover essential expenses, as well as military spending.
Rail services are expected to be disrupted from 21:00 on Thursday until 20:59 on Friday, while the strike in air transport is expected to last for the entirety of Friday.
In local public transport, the impact will vary from city to city. The strike is also expected to affect taxi services throughout Friday, while motorway staff will begin their strike in the evening on Thursday.
Also on Friday, dock workers will mobilise globally against arms trafficking, rearmament policies and the militarisation of ports.
The action has been organised by several unions, including USB in Italy, the CGT in France and other trade union organisations in Greece, Turkey, Morocco and the Basque Country.
According to the organisers, workers from more than 100 ports in 17 countries and four continents have joined the mobilisation.
In Italy the protests will affect, among others, the ports of Genoa, Livorno, Trieste, Civitavecchia, Ancona, Ravenna and Gioia Tauro.
Among USB's key demands is for wages to rise in line with the cost of living, including through the reintroduction of the "scala mobile", a mechanism previously used to automatically adjust wages in line with inflation.
The union is also calling for measures to bring down the costs of essential goods, household bills and rents, and for a reduction in VAT on basic necessities.
According to USB, the government is allocating too many resources to military spending, while funding for health care, education and other public services remains inadequate.

articles.title_orig: Binance Suspends Transactions After It Is Targeted in Biggest-Ever Cyber Heist
articles.title_zh: Binance Suspends Transactions After It Is Targeted in Biggest-Ever Cyber Heist
articles.content_orig:
The digital currency exchange Binance says it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist Thursday, believed to be the largest ever recorded.
The company has suspended all deposits and withdrawals while it works with law enforcement to secure its infrastructure and locate stolen funds.
The hack originated from a compromised laptop, it said, which allowed “an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.”
“The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said late Thursday on X .
About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said.
Binance will “cover all losses” from the hack, it said, adding, “User funds are safe.”
“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice,” it said.
Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars’ worth of digital currencies on the exchange.
Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges.
The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025.
Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change.
“ This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets,” it said.
As word of the hack spread online Thursday, major cryptocurrencies traded lower. Bitcoin was down about 4.3%, while Ethereum lost 4.6% of its value.
Two major stablecoin issuers, Tether and Circle, said they had identified billions of dollars in assets connected to the hackers and had frozen them.
Tether froze more than $1.567 billion worth of its digital currency, CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X .
Jeremy Allaire, CEO of stablecoin issuer Circle, said the company had also frozen hundreds of millions of dollars of assets and was coordinating with law enforcement.
The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence.
Digital currency has been a primary target of hackers for years. In 2025, Coinbase disclosed that thieves had stolen customers’ personal information and tried to extort the company for $20 million . Coinbase refused to pay and offered a bounty for information leading to arrests, instead.
Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, “As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”
Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws. President Donald Trump later granted him a full pardon .
David Ingram is a tech reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Canadian CEO David Morton and daughters shot wife attacked with hammer in Toronto home invasion
articles.title_zh: Canadian CEO David Morton and daughters shot wife attacked with hammer in Toronto home invasion
articles.content_orig:
A Canadian real estate CEO and his two daughters were shot while his wife was struck with a hammer during an invasion inside their multi-million-dollar home in an affluent Toronto neighborhood Thursday morning.
MAC Group boss David Morton and his family were attacked when three masked men stormed into their gated Bridle Path property at around 3:45 a.m., according to The Toronto Sun.
The suspects, who were armed with handguns and a hammer, gained access to the five-bedroom residence through a back door, Toronto Police Service Inspector Kristy Smith told reporters.
Morton, 75, and his daughters, Maggie Zohil-Morton and Cristina Zohil-Morton, confronted the unidentified intruders who were wearing ski masks and hoodies inside the home.
“A struggle ensued during this altercation in which the suspects fired their guns multiple times and one victim was struck with a hammer,” Smith said.
The trio “tried to fight off” the trespassers when they were shot, sources told the outlet.
Morton and one of his daughters were shot in the leg, while the other daughter suffered a gunshot wound under her arm, the outlet reported.
Morton’s wife, Doriana Zohil-Morton, who also serves as the president of the MAC Group, was attacked by one of the hammer-wielding suspects.
Two of the family members suffered “life-altering injuries” and remained hospitalized while the other two sustained non-life-threatening wounds, Smith said.
The family members were not identified by their injuries.
Descriptions of the suspects were not revealed, but officials said they had fled the area in an SUV.
It was not immediately known if anything was stolen from the house during the invasion.
A motive for the attack was not revealed but it is believed they were looking to rob the upscale neighborhood.
“There was a violent interaction. There was a demand made for valuables from within the home. Whether or not they escaped with anything is uncertain at this point,” Smith said.
“An affluent area where people would have things that are sought after would be the motivation for this,” Smith added.
The 5+1 bed, 7 bath is valued at $2.1 million and includes a tennis court, in-ground pool and private gardens to “enhance a luxury lifestyle” according to an online listing.
A nearby home on 10,000 square feet of property is listed for $8.45 million in the ritzy nabe.
Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow called on the community to provide any information about the attack and said there would be added police security around the neighborhood.
“I am deeply troubled by the violent home invasion early this morning in the Bridle Path neighborhood. My thoughts are with the family and their loved ones, who are going through something no family should ever have to face. I am praying for their full recovery,” Chow wrote on X.
The MAC Group is a family-owned company based in Toronto with sub-divisions that specialize in real estate, hospitality and corporate housing.
Morton oversees all divisions of the company as he has 30 years of experience in hospitality and real estate, according to the company’s website.
The couple’s one daughter, Cristina, is listed as the founder of Zohil-Morton law and specializes in Canadian Immigration Law services.
Maggie Zohil-Morton is also listed as an employee for the MAC Group, with her hands on different departments.

articles.title_orig: Putin shuts down Russia’s last independent newspaper
articles.title_zh: Putin shuts down Russia’s last independent newspaper
articles.content_orig:
Emily covers breaking news from all over the world. She previously reported on home news and politics for The Telegraph. You can reach her at emily.smith@telegraph.co.uk
Vladimir Putin has shut down Russia’s last independent newspaper.
The Russian president has ordered the closure of Novaya Gazeta after 33 years. It had previously been placed on a list of state enemies.
The newspaper, which is known for its critical coverage of Russian political and social affairs, has been classed as a “foreign agent” by Moscow .
Sergei Sokolov, the paper’s editor-in-chief, said in a video statement on YouTube: “Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist. The Russian authorities, the Russian special services, have forced the editorial team to end its work.”
The paper was previously placed under investigation, with one of its journalists detained and the home of a senior editor searched.
Mr Sokolov added: “Novaya Gazeta has been killed... On Nov 9 we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave.
“They’re simply throwing us out, giving us barely any time to pack up. The Anna Politkovskaya museum is closing, and portraits of our friends who were killed are being taken down from the walls.”
Mr Sokolov was taken in for questioning earlier this month when his home was searched.
Novaya Gazeta was founded in 1993. It stopped publishing its print edition in 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine.
A European edition of the paper – Novaya Gazeta Europe – was launched from Latvia to avoid censorship, but the website was later blocked by Russia.
Shortly after the invasion, Russia’s Basmanny Court also revoked Novaya Gazeta’s media licence.
Novaya Gazeta’s office, located on Potapovsky Lane, also housed a museum in tribute to Anna Politkovskaya, one of the newspaper’s reporters, who was killed 20 years ago this month when she was shot in front of her apartment in Moscow.
Dmitry Muratov, the newspaper’s former editor and a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, was travelling to Paris on Oct 19 for a commemoration of her death when he discovered the publication was being evicted.
He and Mr Sokolov gathered the paper’s remaining staff on Oct 26 in the basement of the building next door because it was too dangerous to talk in the office, owing to a break-in the previous night.
Staff agreed that it was time to shut down the publication.
“We haven’t died, they’ve killed us – along with the constitution,” Mr Muratov told The Economist. “You can only laugh at Article 29 of the constitution: ‘Censorship is prohibited’.”
He said Novaya Gazeta “was our city”, adding: “They’ve destroyed this city and we’re leaving. But we are not leaving our work.”
A change to the Russian Criminal Code was passed in March 2022, eight days after the invasion of Ukraine, which criminalised the dissemination of “false information” about the Russian military.
Since the law was passed, at least 30 independent Russian media outlets have been forced to close.
Oleg Roldugin, a Novaya Gazeta journalist, was arrested in April and charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”. He pleaded not guilty, according to the state RIA news agency.

articles.title_zh: Scoop: Trump blesses El Salvador strongman's troop surge in Haiti
articles.content_orig:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.
El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele has deployed more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti in a move human rights advocates say could further destabilize the nation and add to rising violence. Trump has reportedly backed Bukele’s deployment of troops, with Bukele claiming his soldiers only intend to rescue four Salvadoran aviation technicians who’d been kidnapped by gangs in Haiti. Back in El Salvador, Bukele’s so-called state of exception, first declared in 2022, has led to the arbitrary arrest of tens of thousands of people, many wrongfully accused of being gang members and denied due process rights while imprisoned in torturous conditions. Bukele spoke from San Salvador Thursday.
President Nayib Bukele : “I told the gangs in Haiti, 'We wiped out the gangs in El Salvador, and we can do the same to you.' In other words, it was a warning. And our mission isn’t to wipe out the gangs in Haiti, but our mission is to rescue our four members. Now, if they don’t hand them over willingly, well, we’ll rescue them by force.”

articles.title_orig: Chinese Executive Close to Nvidia CEO Suspected of Giving China Information
articles.title_zh: Chinese Executive Close to Nvidia CEO Suspected of Giving China Information
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China
US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times.
Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China , prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.

“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in a statement. Megaspeed and customers like it “receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security”.

articles.title_orig: Volkswagen Will Take China-Developed Technology Global In Major Strategy Shift
articles.title_zh: Volkswagen Will Take China-Developed Technology Global In Major Strategy Shift
articles.content_orig:
Volkswagen is done keeping its Chinese software locked inside China. The automaker said its China Electronic Architecture (CEA), built with local electric vehicle maker Xpeng , will underpin next-generation models bound for South America and South Africa. That marks a sharp break from the brand's old "in China, for China" approach.
Now that same software stack is being lined up for Europe. A report summarized by Reuters says Volkswagen is studying whether the China Electronic Architecture could form the basis for future mass-market cars from its VW, Skoda, and Cupra brands in Europe, with the plan still under discussion inside the group.
As reported by Reuters , Volkswagen plans to integrate China-developed technology into South American product lineups starting in 2030 . Volkswagen Group China now uses the China Electronic Architecture in five locally produced all-electric Volkswagen brand models, including the Yuzhong 06 and Yuzhong 07.
Volkswagen Group China laid out the broader package, called VEGA, at a Technology Day event in Hefei. VEGA ties together the China Main Platform, the China Electronic Architecture, and China-developed software and driver-assistance systems into one scalable package for software-defined vehicles across multiple segments.
The China Main Platform targets A-segment battery-electric and plug-in-hybrid models. Volkswagen's stated goal is more than 373 miles of CLTC range and roughly 11 kWh per 62 miles in its most efficient version. Volkswagen says the China-built software could extend further still, with the Europe proposal covering roughly three quarters of the next-generation lineups for VW, Skoda, and Cupra .
Exports of China-developed vehicles are also starting to ramp up around 2026. China-built Volkswagens are already heading to markets such as Mexico and parts of Southeast and Central Asia, with more destinations planned afterward. That export push would run alongside the deeper platform integration planned for 2030.
The architecture trims the number of electronic control units by about 30 percent compared with Volkswagen's older setups. Volkswagen says that reduction is central to cutting development costs and complexity across its lineup.
It's a hardware play as much as a software one. Volkswagen intends to bring the same architecture to plug-in-hybrid and combustion models in China by 2027, which would widen its reach past the battery-electric vehicles where it currently lives and give future gas and hybrid products the same software backbone.
Looking further out, Volkswagen is targeting Level 4 automated driving by 2029, built on a third-generation version of the China Electronic Architecture paired with a Volkswagen-developed C7H control chip. That automated-driving target sits alongside the South America plan and the potential European rollout.
The strategy also threatens to sideline Rivian , Volkswagen's US software partner in a $5.8 billion investment central to CEO Oliver Blume's technology plans. A separate report from German outlet Manager Magazin said core brand chief Thomas Schäfer is weighing a proposal to use China-developed software as the basis for future Volkswagen, Skoda, and Cupra models, which would leave Rivian focused on other group brands even if the joint venture itself stays in place.

articles.title_orig: German president confident of resolving trade disagreements with China
articles.title_zh: German president confident of resolving trade disagreements with China
articles.content_orig:
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is confident Germany and China can resolve trade disagreements.
A recent agreement on limiting hybrid car exports to the European Union showed that even where things were difficult "there is a way to find solutions," Steinmeier said at the start of his meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang in Beijing on Friday.
Steinmeier directly addressed the growing imbalance in bilateral trade relations. Germany's trade deficit with China amounted to just under €90 billion ($100 billion) last year.
"We are coming with the intention of maintaining and strengthening the framework for good economic exchange between our two countries," Steinmeier said.
When there were problems, Germany would work "to solve them together with you through dialogue," he said.
Steinmeier said China remained important as Germany's largest trading partner and praised the country's "breathtaking pace" in technological and economic development.
Li called Steinmeier a "long-time and good friend" of China.
Germany's president holds a largely ceremonial role but frequently speaks on foreign policy and international affairs.
Steinmeier concludes his nearly week-long visit to China on Friday and is also due to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu bloc short of majority as Arab parties secure record seats
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu bloc short of majority as Arab parties secure record seats
articles.content_orig:
Final results from Israel's pivotal legislative election this week showed there was no clear winner, with both of the two main blocs well short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc finished on 53 seats, while the opposition camp, led by the centrist Yashar party of rival Gadi Eisenkot, ended on 48.
Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party remained the largest party, with 27 seats, while the Arab parties secured a record 19 seats between them.
The result means Israel is now set to face a lengthy and likely tricky period of negotiations as party leaders work to form a government. Failure to do so would see Israelis head back to the polls.
Netanyahu has accused Arab parties of "stealing" the election, calling on police and Israel's domestic security service Shin Bet to carry out a "thorough investigation into election fraud."
The Likud party also pushed claims that foreign funding had been used to influence voters in the election. The allegations focused on claims that the Ra'am party had received money from Qatar.
"The ‘Ra’am-gate’ scandal is an earthquake. The Israeli elections have been stolen," Likud said in a statement on Thursday.
Ra'am party leader Mansour Abbas reportedly denied any wrongdoing and said he would welcome an investigation.
In a post on social media, Eisenkot said foreign interference was "unacceptable and extremely serious" and called on Shin Bet to investigate the allegations "fully and immediately, without bias."
Moving forward, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will consult with leaders of the parties elected to the Knesset before assigning the task of trying to form a government to the candidate he believes has the best chance of securing sufficient support to do so.
Under Israeli law, that individual will have 28 days to carry out the job. The president is able to extend this by a maximum of 14 days if necessary.
Should that fail, the president can give a second leader the chance to form a government, this time with a maximum deadline of 28 days. If this second round were also to fail, then the Knesset can request a third candidate be given a go. They would have 14 days to complete the task.
If all attempts fail, another election is called.

articles.title_orig: Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Hacked in Crypto's Biggest Heist
articles.title_zh: Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Hacked in Crypto's Biggest Heist
articles.content_orig:
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has said that about $6.3bn in funds have been stolen in a “security incident” that looks to be the biggest crypto heist in history.
The world’s largest crypto exchange said on Thursday that it had suspended all deposits and withdrawals and that about $3bn in funds had been frozen following the apparent hacking.
Binance said an initial investigation suggested that a hacker had been able to make unauthorised transactions after gaining access to an engineer’s compromised laptop.
The company said it would cover all losses, adding that user funds were “safe”.
“Our teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly,” Binance said in a statement to Al Jazeera.
“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice.”
The company added that it would share a “detailed” technical post-mortem once investigations were complete.
Changpeng Zhao, Binance’s founder and largest shareholder, said earlier that the exchange appeared to have been hacked.
TRM, a blockchain intelligence firm, said in a report that it assessed with “high confidence” that the attack was carried out by North Korea’s hacking unit TraderTraitor, which investigators have linked to the Lazarus Group.
Ari Redbord, TRM’s global head of policy, described the attack as “unprecedented” and a “watershed”.
“When North Korea steals at this scale, the money funds weapons proliferation and other destabilising activity. That makes this a global security issue, not just a crypto theft,” Redbord told Al Jazeera.
The price of Bitcoin, the world’s most popular cryptocurrency, fell about 5 percent following the heist, dropping below $77,000.
“Binance is one of the largest centralised exchanges, and so a blow to confidence in them risks shocking confidence to many retail investors, which could dampen prices of crypto assets,” Sean Foley, an expert in crypto markets at Macquarie University in Sydney, told Al Jazeera.
Foley said the attack highlighted the risks of centralised exchanges and could spur more traders to use decentralised alternatives.
“Any assets held at a centralised exchange are only as safe as the exchange itself, and the larger the exchange’s holdings, the larger a target it becomes,” Foley said.
The Binance hacking dwarfs the previous record for a crypto theft, set in 2025 when North Korean state-backed Lazarus Group carried out a $1.5bn heist on Bybit.
Cybercriminals stole $2.87bn in crypto assets in nearly 150 hacking incidents in 2025, according to the 2026 Crypto Crime Report produced by TRM.
Binance, founded in China by Zhao in 2017, has about $155bn in assets under management, more than any other exchange, according to CoinMarketCap.

articles.title_orig: Global tech rout deepens as US earnings stoke AI spending fears
articles.title_zh: Global tech rout deepens as US earnings stoke AI spending fears
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Iain Withers and Ankur Banerjee
LONDON/SINGAPORE, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Tech shares slumped on Friday and US bonds surged toward their biggest monthly gain in nearly three years, as investors scurried to safety due to worries that huge and rising AI spending may not deliver ‌sufficient returns.
Futures trading pointed to falls on Wall Street later in the session, including a more than 2% drop in the tech-heavy Nasdaq ‌100. That came alongside an out-of-hours plunge of 23% in Intel shares and a drop of 7% in Amazon as their results showed they burned through cash.
Shares in Google parent Alphabet fell 12.6% on ​Wall Street on Thursday and slid a little further after hours, to wipe out a stunning $500 billion in market value, as massive AI spending turned the company's cash flow negative.
European stocks opened down 0.2% on Friday, as the relative lack of big tech stocks helped limit losses. There were falls earlier in Asia led by chipmakers.
Investors are worried about the returns they can expect to make on the massive capital spending needed for the AI buildout and what effect it could have on consumers if ‌price hikes squeeze global demand for devices like smartphones ⁠and PCs. Anthropic's potentially record-breaking IPO could prove the next big test of sentiment.
"The next key milestone will be the Anthropic IPO, to see how that lands. If it's a poor listing, I think that could signal a bit of ⁠weakness going forward," said Jason Da Silva, co-chief investment officer at Arbuthnot Latham.
Nerves were also frayed by a potentially record-breaking hack at Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, which drove down bitcoin and other cryptocurrency prices.
The world's biggest cryptocurrency, bitcoin, hit a six-week low before cutting losses to trade 1.1% lower at $77,876.
"I suspect the negative price action still ​has ​some way to go," said Geoffrey Kendrick, head of digital assets research at Standard ​Chartered. "Only after assets are unfrozen and more detail of the ‌hack emerges will we find a new base."
In commodities, oil prices rose about 2% on Friday and were poised for a fourth monthly gain, as an attack on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz waterway highlighted continuing supply risks from the US-Israeli war on Iran. [O/R]
The Bank of Japan left interest rates on hold, which was expected and did not trigger major currency or bond moves, although in a surprise development the central bank unveiled plans to sharply accelerate exchange-traded fund sales next year.
"While this may initially spook markets, I actually think this is a positive development since the BOJ feels confident ‌enough with the economy and market," said David Chao, global market strategist for Asia-Pacific at ​Invesco.
The central bank declared victory in a nearly 14-year battle to hit its price target and ​signalled vigilance against inflation risks, suggesting the next rate hike could ​come as soon as December.
Tech sector jitters have helped push a rush to bonds, further spurred by the Federal Reserve's ‌decision on Wednesday to keep US interest rates on hold, with ​no firm projection of when it might ​hike next.
Benchmark 10-year US Treasury yields fell around 7 basis points on Friday to 4.92% and were on track for their largest one-month drop since December 2023. Yields fall when bond prices rise.
The risk-averse mood strengthened haven currencies such as the yen and Swiss franc, with the ​yen slightly higher at 157.30 per dollar and the ‌franc at 0.821 to the dollar and not far from a one-month high.
The euro inched up 0.1% to $1.1194 but was set for ​a drop of over 1% in October, its second straight monthly decline.
(Reporting by Iain Withers in London and Tom Westbrook and Ankur ​Banerjee in Singapore; Editing by Tom Hogue, Clarence Fernandez, Stephen Coates, William Maclean)
