articles.title_zh: China seeks to strengthen cooperation with Iceland in Arctic affairs
articles.content_orig:
Chinese President Xi Jinping, center left and Zhang Shengmin, Vice Chairman of the Central Military Commission second from right attend a ceremony in honor of fallen national heroes at the Monument to the People's Heroes to mark Martyrs' Day at Tiananmen Square in Beijing, Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP hide caption
BANGKOK — China's top leaders on Thursday elevated the only remaining general on the commission that oversees the country's military to the Politburo, the top governing body of the Communist Party.
The leaders also adopted a resolution on strengthening self-governance, discipline and anti-corruption in the party, as they seek to extend their grip on power.
During a four-day closed-door meeting, top Communist Party leaders deliberated on and adopted resolutions that will guide the party in the coming years. The meeting comes about a year before President Xi Jinping is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party's leader.
The party elected Gen. Zhang Shengmin, who currently serves as vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, to the Politburo. Xi had earlier purged two of China's top generals, leaving Zhang as the commission's only member besides Xi himself. It also left the Politburo without any representatives from the People's Liberation Army.
Zhang also holds a position overseeing internal discipline for the military, serving as deputy secretary of the CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection.
The party said in a summary of the resolution that the tasks facing it were "increasingly arduous," such as "uniting and leading the people to safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."
It said it must step up its self-governance, which involves rooting out corruption and maintaining ideological purity.
The party should, "with an eye on enhancing its long-term governance capacity, maintain its progressive nature and purity, and its close, flesh-and-blood ties with the people," according to a summary of the resolution from the official Xinhua News Agency.
Xi has championed anti-corruption since coming to power in 2012, and has sustained a crackdown on officials for more than a decade. However, analysts say the focus now also includes underperforming officials.
Party members also reviewed the earlier purges of top members and military officials, confirming the personnel changes.
The plenum meeting revealed wider-than-expected purges, according to analysis by Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at Asia Policy who studies Chinese politics. He calculated an attendance rate of 74 percent, the lowest since the times of former leader Mao Zedong, who ran political purges regularly.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu alleges stolen election as he seeks political survival amid uncertainty
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu alleges stolen election as he seeks political survival amid uncertainty
articles.content_orig:
Danny Danon joins 'Fox & Friends First' to discuss Israel holding its first election since the October 7 attacks. He analyzes the future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and reacts to President Donald Trump's call for Netanyahu's re-election.
TEL AVIV, Israel: Israel's two Arab parties are in a position to have a say in who the country's next prime minister and government will be — but not if Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has anything to do with it, after he alleged serious criminal activities took place during voting in the Arab areas of the nation.
The two parties were projected to win a combined 19 Knesset seats, according to preliminary results. However, both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud-led right-wing bloc and the opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s centrist bloc fell short of the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
On Wednesday, Prime Minister Netanyahu wrote on X that Israel’s election had been "stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state," alleging serious criminal offenses, including bribery, threats, violence, forgery and the use of prohibited software to mobilize voters.
NETANYAHU GAINS OVERNIGHT AS ISRAEL ELECTION HEADS TOWARD POLITICAL DEADLOCK
People cast their votes at a polling station during Israel's legislative election in the Arab town of Taibe in northern Israel on Oct. 27, 2026. (Gil Cohen-Magen/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Images)
"The Likud party is transferring to the police, the Shin Bet and the Central Elections Committee hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence regarding election theft in many Arab polling stations," he wrote.
He cited allegations of thousands of envelopes containing cash and Ra’am ballot slips, threats and violence against polling station staff, multiple votes cast behind the voting curtain, voting under multiple identities, discrepancies between the number of ballot envelopes and the number of voters, the use of prohibited voter-mobilization software and other offenses.
"We demand from the police and the Shin Bet a thorough investigation into the election theft by the Arab parties and the full prosecution of the criminals. We demand from the Central Elections Committee an immediate response to investigate these criminal offenses that have severely damaged the integrity of the elections in Israel and the election results," he added.
In a letter addressed to Yesh Atid lawmaker Vladimir Beliak, Acting Central Elections Committee Director-General Dean Livne wrote that the elections "were conducted lawfully" and that, "to the best of my knowledge, there is no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity," the Times of Israel reported . He also acknowledged that the request for an investigation concerned classified information whose veracity had not yet been determined.
A boy sits on his bicycle next to a campaign banner of Netanyahu's Likud Party, ahead of the Israeli parliamentary election, in Bnei Brak, Israel, October 25, 2026. (Nir Elias/Reuters)
The political makeup of the Arab parties includes the Joint List, which brings together three parties: Hadash, a predominantly Arab-Jewish left-wing party rooted in Israel’s communist movement, and the Arab nationalist parties Ta’al and Balad. With over 90% of ballots counted, the alliance was projected to win 12 seats.
The other Arab party, the United Arab List (Ra’am), led by Mansour Abbas and affiliated with the Southern Branch of the Islamic Movement in Israel, was projected to win seven seats.
Arab citizens make up approximately 21% of Israel’s population. Turnout in this election reached a near record high of between 75% and 80%.
"They are a political force to be reckoned with," Dahlia Scheindlin, a former policy fellow at the Mitvim Institute and a senior analyst at Haaretz, told Fox News Digital.
NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reacts after filling out his ballot before voting at a polling station in Jerusalem on Oct. 27, 2026, on the day of Israel's legislative election. (Yonatan Sindel/Pool via Reuters)
Scheindlin said that Netanyahu framed his campaign around the claim that the opposition is prepared to form a government dependent on Arab parties’ support, which he argues would lead to the establishment of a Palestinian state that would become a terror state and ultimately bring about Israel’s destruction.
"This is the most consistent message, and he never stopped saying it, including on election day," she said.
Scheindlin said that the issue had become politically sensitive, prompting leading Zionist opposition parties to pledge not to cooperate with the Arab parties.
"They have sworn they would not build a coalition that depends on Arab votes, either from within the coalition or from outside it. If they receive any help, they will have to break that promise," she added.
It is not inconceivable, though highly unlikely, that Netanyahu could reach out to one of the Arab parties to explore the possibility of cooperation , Scheindlin said.
People gather near a pre-election campaign banner featuring leaders of the Joint List, ahead of Israel's national election, in Nazareth, Israel, Oct. 10, 2026. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)
ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW
Dr. Arik Rudnitzky, a researcher in the Israel Democracy Institute’s Arab Society in Israel Program, said that Arab parties had historically remained in the opposition and had not joined governing coalitions.
During the governments of Yitzhak Rabin and, later, Shimon Peres in the 1990s, Arab parties provided a parliamentary safety net from outside the coalition. This enabled the government to remain in office and complete its term even after it effectively became a minority government amid opposition to the Oslo Accords , as the Haredi Shas Party left the government.
"Historically, Arab parties were always in the opposition for many reasons. It was quite uncommon to believe Arab parties could [support] the government. It’s a novelty of recent years, plus the fact that their political strength in terms of the number of seats was not as significant as it is today," Rudnitzky said.
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar ("Straight") Party, waves an Israeli flag onstage following the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election in Tel Aviv, Israel, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (Ariel Schalit/AP Photo)
Demographic changes alone do not explain the Arab parties’ growing political strength, Rudnitzky said; shifting voting patterns have also played a role.
"In the past, Arab voters supported both Arab and Jewish parties. In the 1980s and 1990s, approximately half voted for Jewish parties," he continued.
Rudnitzky said historical developments, the impact of the Oslo Accords and the entry of new Arab representatives into the Knesset contributed to a gradual shift away from Jewish parties, with more Arab voters turning to Arab parties.
"Today, we can say that between 85% and 90% of Arab voters support Arab parties. This is the main reason for their increased political strength," he added.
Any support Arab parties might provide to a prospective coalition would come in exchange for political concessions, Rudnitzky said. Their demands would likely include a government decision and a plan to combat crime in Arab communities, as well as a new socioeconomic development plan for the Arab sector involving budget allocations.
Ultimately, he said, such arrangements would involve allocating public goods and resources in exchange for political support. "There is no free lunch in politics. Every collaboration, either within a coalition or from the outside, has its political price."

articles.title_orig: US Lawmakers Condemn Lavrov’s G20 Visit as Russia Continues Attacks on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: US Lawmakers Condemn Lavrov’s G20 Visit as Russia Continues Attacks on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in Atlanta on Friday, Oct. 30 for the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting despite objections from US lawmakers and European allies. Moscow plans to challenge Western sanctions as Washington prepares new peace talks involving Ukraine and Russia.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in the US on Friday, Oct. 30, for a G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, despite calls from US lawmakers to bar him from the country while Moscow continues its war and deadly attacks on Ukrainian civilians.
Lavrov’s arrival, reported by Russia’s state-owned TASS news agency, comes days after Russian strikes killed civilians across Ukraine, including 14 people at a railway station in Dnipro.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The Kremlin’s top diplomat, under US sanctions since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, is expected to use the Oct. 30-31 gathering to criticize Western sanctions against Moscow, according to Russia’s Foreign Ministry.
Republican Rep. Don Bacon sharply condemned Lavrov’s visit, calling for the Russian foreign minister to be barred from entering the US while Moscow continues its deadly attacks on Ukrainian cities.
“Lavrov should not be allowed in the country. As long as Putin is waging war against Ukraine and bombing cities, Russian leaders should not be welcomed in any of these forums. They lead a pariah state,” Bacon wrote on X on Wednesday, Oct. 28.
Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, also sharply criticized Trump’s approach to Moscow, demanding that Washington stop extending diplomatic legitimacy to Putin’s regime while Russian forces continue killing Ukrainian civilians.
“Donald Trump needs to wake up,” Shaheen said in an Oct. 8 CNN interview. “He needs to understand that courting favor with Vladimir Putin is not good for America.”
Shaheen, who joined 13 bipartisan senators in calling for Putin and other sanctioned Russian officials to be barred from G20 events on US soil, urged the administration to increase pressure on Moscow rather than reward it with international recognition.
In their letter to Trump , the senators questioned why Russia should receive diplomatic legitimacy while continuing its deadly attacks on Ukraine’s cities and civilian infrastructure.
The bipartisan criticism comes just days before the Nov. 3 US midterm elections, with the Trump administration facing questions over its approach to Moscow amid continued Russian strikes on Ukraine.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Lavrov would use his appearance to argue against economic sanctions and other trade restrictions, portraying them as instruments of pressure.
The Russian delegation also intends to promote Moscow’s vision of a multipolar international order.
The visit comes as Washington prepares new trilateral talks involving the US, Ukraine, and Russia, expected in November in Abu Dhabi.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is hosting the G20 gathering, which will address major international disputes alongside energy security, trade and global supply chains.
The meeting also precedes the Dec. 14-15 G20 leaders’ summit at President Trump’s Doral resort in Miami, to which Putin has been invited. His attendance remains unconfirmed.
According to the State Department’s delegation list, Lavrov is attending alongside foreign ministers from major NATO and European countries, including Germany’s Johann Wadephul, France’s Jean-Noël Barrot, Poland’s Radosław Sikorski, Canada’s Anita Anand, and Turkey’s Hakan Fidan.
Other participants include EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, Britain’s Ed Miliband, Australia’s Penny Wong, India’s Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, and Japan’s Toshimitsu Motegi.
China is represented by Executive Vice Foreign Minister Ma Zhaoxu rather than Foreign Minister Wang Yi.
Ukraine was not invited, although it had participated in previous G20 meetings as a guest. US officials said the decision reflected a policy of limiting invitations to formal members. South Africa was also excluded amid tensions with Washington.
Russia’s participation has unsettled some Western allies, who have questioned the invitation while Moscow intensifies its attacks on Ukraine.
The G20 meeting opens as Washington seeks renewed diplomatic engagement with Moscow, while Ukraine and its European partners continue pressing for stronger sanctions and security guarantees.

articles.title_orig: Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history
articles.title_zh: Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history
articles.content_orig:
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record.
The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses".
Early checks show the incident may have involved an engineer's laptop that had been compromised, which allowed an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said.
Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor.
Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack.
Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record".
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen.
The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack.
For the last few years North Korea-linked operatives have focussed on attacking cryptocurrency companies for large thefts of digital tokens.
Western security agencies have previously said stolen funds are used to finance North Korea's nuclear weapons and missile development programs.
The regime has denied any involvement in hacks in the past.
Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets.
Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."
The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue.
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop.
"That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions," he said in a statement.
"To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual. So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak."
He said a detailed "post-mortem" would be shared once the investigation was complete.
Check Point's Dave said this attack also resembled a hack on crypto exchange platform Bitget in September in which $388m (£289m) was lost: "This implies that attackers no longer need the vault keys. They target the systems and people with authority to use them."
In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets.
"Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said.
Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack.
World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds.
Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation.
Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue.
Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.

articles.title_orig: Blockchain analysis firm TRM says North Korea behind Binance crypto theft
articles.title_zh: Blockchain analysis firm TRM says North Korea behind Binance crypto theft
articles.content_orig:
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has said that about $6.3bn in funds have been stolen in a “security incident” that looks to be the biggest crypto heist in history.
The world’s largest crypto exchange said on Thursday that it had suspended all deposits and withdrawals and that about $3bn in funds had been frozen following the apparent hacking.
Binance said an initial investigation suggested that a hacker had been able to make unauthorised transactions after gaining access to an engineer’s compromised laptop.
The company said it would cover all losses, adding that user funds were “safe”.
“Our teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly,” Binance said in a statement to Al Jazeera.
“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice.”
The company added that it would share a “detailed” technical post-mortem once investigations were complete.
Changpeng Zhao, Binance’s founder and largest shareholder, said earlier that the exchange appeared to have been hacked.
TRM, a blockchain intelligence firm, said in a report that it assessed with “high confidence” that the attack was carried out by North Korea’s hacking unit TraderTraitor, which investigators have linked to the Lazarus Group.
Ari Redbord, TRM’s global head of policy, described the attack as “unprecedented” and a “watershed”.
“When North Korea steals at this scale, the money funds weapons proliferation and other destabilising activity. That makes this a global security issue, not just a crypto theft,” Redbord told Al Jazeera.
The price of Bitcoin, the world’s most popular cryptocurrency, fell about 5 percent following the heist, dropping below $77,000.
“Binance is one of the largest centralised exchanges, and so a blow to confidence in them risks shocking confidence to many retail investors, which could dampen prices of crypto assets,” Sean Foley, an expert in crypto markets at Macquarie University in Sydney, told Al Jazeera.
Foley said the attack highlighted the risks of centralised exchanges and could spur more traders to use decentralised alternatives.
“Any assets held at a centralised exchange are only as safe as the exchange itself, and the larger the exchange’s holdings, the larger a target it becomes,” Foley said.
The Binance hacking dwarfs the previous record for a crypto theft, set in 2025 when North Korean state-backed Lazarus Group carried out a $1.5bn heist on Bybit.
Cybercriminals stole $2.87bn in crypto assets in nearly 150 hacking incidents in 2025, according to the 2026 Crypto Crime Report produced by TRM.
Binance, founded in China by Zhao in 2017, has about $155bn in assets under management, more than any other exchange, according to CoinMarketCap.

articles.title_orig: Asia Stocks Under Pressure, Haven Bid Boosts Bonds: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Asia Stocks Under Pressure, Haven Bid Boosts Bonds: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
TOKYO – Asian shares were trading mixed Friday, as worries about the future of artificial intelligence grew after Alphabet's stock drop dragged on U.S. markets.
Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 dropped 2.3% in afternoon trading to 63,155.94. At the end of its two-day monetary policy board meeting, the Bank of Japan decided to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 1.25%. That was widely expected because the central bank raised the rate last month.
The U.S. has been pressuring Japan to raise rates because of concerns about the weakening yen. In currency trading, the U.S. dollar inched up to 157.67 Japanese yen from 157.65 yen. The euro cost $1.1186, up from $1.1181.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.2% to 8,908.10. South Korea's Kospi declined nearly 4% to 5,701.71, as shares in SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics both slipped.
Shares related to the great market interest in AI have tended to be volatile, because some issues, including chip makers, get pushed up because of that interest, but then may decline because of worries about supplies, for instance.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng added 1.7% to 23,359.06, while the Shanghai Composite lost 0.4% to 3,636.60.
On Wall Street, the S&P 500 fell 0.3% for its first loss in four days , even though the wide majority of stocks rose within the index and across Wall Street. The Nasdaq composite tumbled 1.4%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 132 points, or 0.3%.
Alphabet is one of the most influential stocks on Wall Street because it’s one of the largest, and the Class A shares of its stock fell 12.6% for their worst day since they began trading more than 20 years ago.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 23.59 points to 7,720.39 Thursday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 132.54 to 52,342.56, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 365.13 to 26,184.72.
In the bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.94% from 5.05% late Wednesday. It’s been generally pulling back since it topped 5.30% earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002.
In energy trading, benchmark U.S. crude gained 1.15% to $103.17 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, edged up 1.05% to $116.09 a barrel.
AP Business Writer Stan Choe contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Carney, top EU official push Canada associate membership and wider alliance against Trump threats
articles.title_zh: Carney, top EU official push Canada associate membership and wider alliance against Trump threats
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is hosting European Union leaders in Montreal on Friday as he looks to deepen ties with like-minded leaders in the face of an increasingly protectionist United States.
But the rise of nationalist political forces in Europe could make that more difficult in the years to come.
The 21st Canada-EU summit, which wraps Friday, is aimed at forging a stronger alliance between Canada and the 27-member bloc in the face of an unpredictable and volatile White House.
On Thursday, both Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stressed the two sides' shared values as they pitched an "alliance for the future" based on deeper trade and security ties.
Carney says Canada is working to become an 'associate member' as he hosts EU leaders in Montreal
EU dropping associate membership title for its closer alliance with Canada
But shifting political winds on the continent could test that alliance, notably in France and Germany — heavyweights within the bloc.
In France, presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally is leading in polls ahead of the spring 2027 election. Le Pen, an advocate for strict immigration limits, has criticized the EU-Canada trade pact.
While in Germany, the far-right and isolationist Alternative for Germany (AfD) continues to gain ground in regional parliaments and national polls.
Asked Thursday if he has concerns about dealing with a potentially different political makeup, Carney praised the EU's adherence to democratic values.
Canada forging 'alliance for the future' with EU as an 'associate member,' Carney says
"One of Europe's strengths is democracy, freedom and a core belief in the rule of law. There will always be different governments, governments of different stripes in Europe," he told reporters.
"Over the course of decades, the European Union has continued to develop, and strengthen, throughout, and be enriched by the national democratic processes of those countries."
Carney also downplayed the notion he was looking to secure commitments with the EU before the French election.
"We're not tying it to any political cycle, but to the fundamentals of what they deliver … for Canadians," he said.
Far right gains ground in Europe as Canada pivots from Trump to EU
Despite some objections from EU members, von der Leyen has pitched making Canada the first associate member of the bloc. Carney has welcomed a more expansive alliance across the Atlantic.
That appeared to anger U.S. President Donald Trump who said if he interpreted the move as a "hostile act," he might stop trading with Europe "on many things."
Asked earlier this week about the summit potentially attracting retaliation from Trump or right-wing leaders in Europe, a senior Canadian government official told reporters the gathering isn't directed against anyone but reflected deep interests between Canada and the EU.
As the two-day summit winds down, the Canadian and European sides are expected to release a joint statement on Friday with a number of new commitments.
A draft version of the statement seen by CBC News commits to reinforcing "a predictable trade environment," deepening collaboration in critical mineral supply chains, countering cyberattacks and continued support for Ukraine.
Both sides are also promising to launch negotiations toward deeper participation in Erasmus, the European Union's student and youth exchange program.
Catharine Tunney is a reporter with CBC's Parliament Hill bureau, where she covers national security and the RCMP. She worked previously for CBC in Nova Scotia. You can reach her at catharine.tunney@cbc.ca
With files from Marina von Stackelberg

articles.title_orig: China expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officials
articles.title_zh: China expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officials
articles.content_orig:
The unprecedented number of empty seats at the fifth plenum – a symbol of expulsions – serve as a symbol for the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping
China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering , which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.
The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified , taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.
Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.
A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.
The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi is expected to secure a fourth term as leader of the party, making him the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong.
The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

articles.title_orig: Chinese Embassy in Mexico slams US officials’ malicious smears against China-Mexico cooperation
articles.title_zh: Chinese Embassy in Mexico slams US officials’ malicious smears against China-Mexico cooperation
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — A top aide to U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said in a phone call Monday night that prosecutors had made a “f---up” in a high-profile criminal case against two former FBI officials , an agent who’s been investigating the case testified Thursday.
The former officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, were initially charged last week with making false statements to Congress about their level of knowledge about an investigation of Hunter Biden’s laptop.
A sworn affidavit attached to the complaint by Special Agent Ryan Witt cited a congressional staffer who was present for both Floris’ and Benavides’ testimony — but it turns out the person was only present for Benavides’, Witt testified at a preliminary hearing on whether there’s probable cause to charge the pair.
Witt told Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui that he called the congressional staffer on Monday and was later joined on the call by Pirro aide Carlton Davis and Pirro, the top federal prosecutor for Washington, D.C.
Audio of that conversation was turned over to Benavides’ attorney, Ron Safer, who read parts of the exchange in court and asked Witt whether it was accurate.
At one point, Davis told the staffer, House Judiciary Committee general counsel Steve Castor, “This is our f---up,” and asked for his help finding someone who had been present for the testimony, Witt confirmed.
Witt added that he still has not been able to speak to anyone who was there.
Later Monday night, prosecutors filed what they called a superseding criminal complaint and a new affidavit, neither of which was signed by any law enforcement officer or judge. Faruqui tossed the complaint on Tuesday.
On Wednesday, one of the attorneys for the defense asked Witt if it was unusual for a case alleging defendants made false statements to use an affidavit containing false statements — a question the judge cut off.
Davis, who is listed as a special counsel in Pirro’s office, was involved in the failed effort to indict six sitting members of Congress over their comments in a social media video where they urged members of the military not to follow illegal orders. Davis previously worked as a Republican staffer on several committees, including the House Select Committee on Benghazi.
Witt was on the stand in the case for a third day.
He testified Tuesday that he was assigned to the case in July after FBI Director Kash Patel sent a letter directing the Kansas City, Missouri, office to look into certain people, including Floris.
The direction came a day after President Donald Trump delivered an Oval Office address in which he complained that “rogue bureaucrats” had suppressed information about China’s efforts to interfere in the 2020 election, which he falsely claims was “stolen.”
Both Floris and Benavides were involved in FBI efforts to secure the election and have long been targets of criticism from Trump’s allies.
Witt said he was unhappy with the assignment, in part because “I had concerns that this would be viewed as political.”
Witt said Wednesday that top FBI brass, including Patel, had been checking on progress in the case through in-person meetings, videoconferences and updates pushed through their special agent in charge. Witt said both FBI deputy directors — Chris Raia and Andrew Bailey, who recently resigned — were involved.
“The evidence in this case speaks for itself [as] to the effect that kind of pressure has on sensitive investigations like this one,” Floris’ attorney Mary Dohrmann told the judge Thursday.
She said there were other mistakes in the affidavit as well, and that some of the false statements her client was alleged to have made were presented stripped of necessary context.
Safer, Benavides’ attorney, told Faruqui that in most instances, calling something a political prosecution is a talking point, but not in this case.
“That is the price we pay to allow politics to infect the process,” he said.
The judge said he plans to issue a written ruling Monday morning.
Ryan J. Reilly is a justice reporter for NBC News.
Tanish Bijur is an intern on the Justice and National Security Unit
Dareh Gregorian is a politics reporter for NBC News.

A pair of Gemini app updates today brings the latest design to all Android devices, while file generation sees a big upgrade.
The latest Gemini overlay design applies a heavy blur effect over the bar. It’s hard to make out the boundaries of the pill, while there are way more tiny specks and swirls of color. PDF preview and editing are supported on gemini.google.com and the mobile apps, while Google Docs, Google Sheets, Google Slides, Markdown files, TXT files, and code are web-only.

articles.title_orig: Canada and Europe share challenge of diversifying without antagonizing US and China
articles.title_zh: Canada and Europe share challenge of diversifying without antagonizing US and China
articles.content_orig:
MONTREAL — There’s one thing the European Union and Canada want to avoid with their new alliance: stoking new fury from Washington and Beijing.
Officials have been under pressure to check off everything they said they would do at the last summit and on Friday will unveil the areas they plan to focus on over the next year, as they intensify their transatlantic cooperation. But don’t expect a parade of new deals.
“Canada has objectives where they need our technology — so you can build a beautiful relationship if you focus on it,” one senior EU official told POLITICO about shared challenges in diversifying away from the U.S. and China. The official was granted anonymity to speak candidly about sensitive diplomatic negotiations between Brussels and Ottawa.
One of the core EU interests in Canada, the official explained, is a chance for the bloc to diversify its supply of critical raw materials and sources of energy to further reduce its dependence on China and Russia, respectively.
“They have most of what we need,” the official said about Canadian minerals. “There’s also a huge opportunity to bring Canadian fossil fuels and gas to the EU.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed the controversy over whether the EU should label the relationship with Canada as an “associate membership,” saying on Thursday it was a sideshow to what’s been billed as a landmark summit.
Earlier this week, Germany, France, Greece and other countries opposed the definition in a joint EU-Canada statement to be issued in Montreal. That came after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen put forward the “associate membership” label in September.
But Carney told reporters on Thursday that the new alliance wasn’t “a marketing exercise” and that the name doesn’t matter. “What matters is that the complementarities of our two jurisdictions strengthen our sovereignty, strengthen Europe’s sovereignty, various strategic autonomies, critical minerals, energy, other aspects — AI,” he said.
A tricky political road lies ahead as Carney and von der Leyen make moves to draw the EU and Canada closer in a partnership that doesn’t include its southern neighbor. They’ll need to  tiptoe forward with an “association without accession” work plan in the last years of the U.S. President Donald Trump’s time in office.
Montreal’s historic Fairmont The Queen Elizabeth hotel was a hub of summit activity on Thursday, beginning with a morning spectacle of von der Leyen heading out of the hotel in runners, taking staff out for a walking meeting. EU commissioners and Canadian Cabinet ministers sailed in and out of the hotel’s perfumed lobby, greeting colleagues.
Jet-lagged Europeans, along with Canadian officials and lobbyists, commiserated over what they saw as poor summit organization, spread across multiple locations.
The debate over membership semantics became a luncheon laugh line when European Council President António Costa endorsed Von der Leyen’s offer to Canada before joking the final designation is “subject to revision”
Then, between servings of frisée salad and roast salmon, Costa struck a diplomatic balance.
“Tomorrow, the European Union and Canada will launch an alliance for the future of Europe,” he said, invoking German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s preferred label and a term Carney has also used to describe the relationship. But Costa also backed von der Leyen’s “ambition” of Canada as an “associate member” of the EU, admitting the term might not matter in the end.
By mid-afternoon, Carney seemed to come around to the term, recognizing the work underway to deepen relations as “an alliance for the future, with Canada as an associate member, between Canada and the European Union.”
The two sides are expected to announce a wrap on talks on a new digital trade agreement on Friday, ending negotiations that were launched in the spring. Other anticipated outcomes include an agreement between the European Investment Bank and Canada, geared to allow the bloc to fund Canadian critical minerals projects.
Eleven EU commissioners in town to “further an agenda” is no small accomplishment, Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told reporters. “It’s a historic moment that we need to seize.”
AI and energy companies are expected to be major beneficiaries of an enhanced EU–Canada relationship, making the absences of European Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen and Canadian Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson noteworthy.
Zoya Sheftalovich contributed to this report from Montreal.

articles.title_orig: Crypto firms freeze more than $2.5bn in funds as Binance investigates potential hack
articles.title_zh: Crypto firms freeze more than $2.5bn in funds as Binance investigates potential hack
articles.content_orig:
World’s largest crypto exchange said it had not confirmed whether funds had been pilfered
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday it is investigating reports of a potential security issue as its founder said the incident “does look like a hack on Binance”. The company said cryptocurrency firms had frozen about $3bn in funds by Thursday evening.
It was not immediately clear the extent of the damage hackers might have been able to accomplish and Binance had not explicitly confirmed that funds had been pilfered, but stablecoin issuers quickly froze funds Thursday evening.
“Our teams continue to work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets,” Binance said in a statement posted to social media. “User funds are safe.”
Stablecoin providers Tether and Circle each said they froze funds Thursday in response to the incident.
Jeremy Allaire, co-founder and CEO of Circle, wrote on X that the company had frozen more than an equivalent of $800m in currency associated with the incident “in coordination with law enforcement”. Paolo Ardoino, the CEO of Tether, said on X that the company froze the equivalent of more than $1.5bn in currency related to “a potential Binance exchange hack”.
The price of bitcoin dropped 3.2% Thursday afternoon to under $79,000.
Binance was founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao, who in 2023 pleaded guilty to a felony related to his failure to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as CEO. Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.
Zhao posted on X on Thursday that “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack on Binance”. He added that while he doesn’t manage Binance anymore, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s election ended in deadlock. Here are four ways out
articles.title_zh: Israel’s election ended in deadlock. Here are four ways out
articles.content_orig:
Israel faces weeks, possibly months, of political limbo after final results show there’s no clear winner in its elections .
Neither of the two main blocs – one led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party, the other led by the centrist Yashar party of his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot – have reached the required 61-seat majority to form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament.
So how could a new government be formed?
Certainly, it does not look easy, with deep-rooted political and ideological divisions making any seemingly straightforward coalition almost impossible.
Still, it can be done, even if the result is a tenuous alliance that survives little more than a year or so in office. If party leaders are unable to figure it out in the 12 weeks they will have available, then Israelis will be back at the polls.
Here’s some potential scenarios that could avoid that.
On paper, the opposition’s surest path to unseat Netanyahu is built on Jewish-Arab cooperation. And that is its biggest obstacle.
Two of the opposition bloc’s right-wing party leaders, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman, oppose any government that depends on the two Arab parties in parliament – the Joint List and Raam – whether it’s from inside the coalition, or as outside supporters of a minority government. The two leaders have hardened their positions since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023.
Only one government in Israel’s history has enjoyed the full participation of an Arab party. Raam was part of an eight-party coalition that succeeded in ousting Netanyahu in 2021, but it collapsed just after a year in office.
Even without forming a government, the opposition parties could still work together and leverage their parliamentary majority to replace the Knesset speaker, along with other key positions, and thereby constrain Netanyahu’s caretaker government as it continued in power. But the prospects of assembling a coalition to replace him as Israel’s leader remain highly complicated and politically charged.
Another option would see the implosion of the two blocs in favor of a unity government. Netanyahu’s Likud party would certainly be involved, along with some of his existing coalition partners, as well as – crucially – at least one party from the opposition bloc.
Netanyahu, in this case, is believed to be willing to part ways with his far-right National Security Minister Ben-Gvir – but not from far-right Finance Minister Bezazel Smotrich and the ultra-Orthodox parties.
Eisenkot , however, has ruled out sitting with Netanyahu, and it would be seen by many Israelis desperate to see the back of ‘Bibi’ as an act of betrayal if he were to change his mind.
Another scenario could see Netanyahu encouraging defections from opposition parties or individual lawmakers.
But all four opposition bloc party leaders – Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman and Yair Golan – have declared they will not sit with him. And with Netanyahu’s bloc a full eight seats short, persuading eight individual defectors sets a high bar.
While all these possibilities are being discussed in the background, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will hold a very public round of consultations with the leaders of the parties that have made it into parliament.
Once he has solicited their opinions, he will task one of those leaders with the job of trying to form a government. Arab parties are expected to voice their support for Eisenkot, so the Yashar leader could be asked to go first.
Whoever gets the nod will have 28 days to complete the job, with a possible 14-day extension if needed.
If it all comes to nothing, the president will ask a second leader to have a go. They get 28 days only to sort it out.
After that, a majority of Knesset members could ask the president to task a third candidate, who then has 14 days to build a coalition.
If none of these produce a breakthrough, there will be another election.
The person who appears best-placed to navigate this timetable is Netanyahu. As caretaker prime minister, he can afford to wait: If main rival Eisenkot gets the first shot – and fails – the mandate is likely to pass to him. And if he fails as well, the political deadlock seems certain to lead Israel to another round of elections – with Netanyahu remaining caretaker for months, until another government is formed.
A repeat election – which would happen no earlier than next spring – is a real possibility, as these results look set to return Israel to a state of political paralysis and what would be the seventh general election in eight years.

articles.title_orig: Bukele's gang offensive goes abroad as El Salvador rushes troops to Haiti
articles.title_zh: Bukele's gang offensive goes abroad as El Salvador rushes troops to Haiti
articles.content_orig:
El Salvadoran military vehicles arrive in the Haitian capital Port-au-Prince
El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti as part of a mission to retrieve four nationals who went missing in the Caribbean country almost two weeks ago.
The "robust deployment" was communicated by El Salvador President Nayib Bukele to the Prime Minister of Haiti Alix Didier Fils-Aime earlier this week, the foreign ministry of El Salvador said in a statement on Wednesday.
Bukele said the soldiers would also assist ongoing "security efforts against gangs in Haiti", the statement continued.
Tensions between the two central American countries have escalated over the disappearance of the four air force technicians working as part of a UN-backed anti-gang organisation in Haiti.
The four soldiers with the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) were travelling back to their base in an armoured vehicle when they were ambushed in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets.
No gang has so far claimed responsibility.
The Salvadoran foreign ministry said the "large-scale operation" was "supported by various countries and international organisations".
Earlier this week, Haiti handed four bodies over to special forces claiming they belonged to those of the missing servicemen, but Bukele said they did not match.
He said one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's military uniform.
Bukele threatened last week in an X post to wipe out Haiti's gangs, saying he will replicate action he has taken in El Salvador, if they did not release the Salvadorans.
In October last year , the UN Security Council approved expanded powers for the GSF to tackle worsening gang violence in Haiti.
The multinational force has struggled to penetrate areas where gangs hold sway. More than 5,700 people were killed in gang-related violence in Haiti this year, the UN says, and armed gangs control much of the capital.
Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of President Jovenel MoÃ¯se in 2021.

articles.title_orig: Dow loses 100 points, S&P 500 snaps 3-day advance as Alphabet and Caterpillar tank: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow loses 100 points, S&P 500 snaps 3-day advance as Alphabet and Caterpillar tank: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Alphabet shares plunged the most since Google went public in 2004, dropping 13% on Thursday, wiping out roughly $500 billion in market cap.
In its earnings announcement late Wednesday, Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion for the third quarter, compared to the $2.7 billion analysts expected. The Google parent maintained its full year capital expenditure guidance of between $195 billion and $205 billion.
Microsoft , meanwhile, traded largely flat as investors focused on the tech giants' latest spending and free cash flow numbers in the third-quarter earnings report.
Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, which was 30% higher than a year ago, but below analyst projections of $50.67 billion. Free cash flow fell 27% to $18.63 billion but remained positive.
The earnings reports come as investors scrutinize AI spending plans of tech companies and are focusing on the returns on those investments.
"Microsoft is building out its architecture in a measured way and as such contains fewer surprises," Ben Barringer, global head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said on Thursday. "Alphabet, by contrast, saw its share price hit after hours as a result of a fairly messy set of results and a poorly handled earnings call" .
Alphabet's biggest source of revenue, search advertising, grew 12% in the September quarter to $63.35 billion, but missed analyst expectations, adding further pressure to the company's shares.
Philipp Schindler, Alphabet's chief business officer, said the impact on the search business was partly because of lower monetization within the company's AI Mode. He added that Alphabet is now "scaling" ads within its AI Overviews and AI Mode products, including in international markets.
Google's search business has faced headwinds from the rise of other AI chatbots like OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude. People may be carrying out more search queries outside Google. Gemini, Google's own AI chatbot, has failed to keep pace.
"The problem for Google is it faces an innovator's dilemma and doesn't know whether to protect its core business or look to join the disruption. As such, Google has lost its edge with Gemini and is behind peers on agentic AI," Barringer said.
Google's dominant market share in the search business, however, could ultimately give it a leg up over its peers, Rosenblatt Securities analyst Scott Devitt said.
"I don't think it's a sea change," Devitt told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Thursday. "If it's a problem for Alphabet, it's a problem for any consumer-facing AI agent or LLM as well. And so, it's a problem that I think is ultimately going to be resolved. And when it does, Alphabet, with its 4 billion search customers that become AI customers, is in an enviable position."
- CNBC's Robert Hum, Samantha Subin, Jordan Novet and Caleigh Keating contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Rivian Beats Estimates as R2 SUV Becomes Its Top-Selling EV
articles.title_zh: Rivian Beats Estimates as R2 SUV Becomes Its Top-Selling EV
articles.content_orig:
Rivian Automotive beat Wall Street's third-quarter earnings expectations as it ramped up production of its new R2 entry-level SUV that the company has promised investors will lead it to profitability.
Here's how Rivian performed in the period ended Sept. 30, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:
Shares of Rivian were up roughly 7% during afterhours trading Thursday, after hitting a new 52-week low of $11.38 earlier in the day. The stock closed at $11.45 a share, down 1.9%
The electric vehicle maker also revised its 2026 guidance to mark expected improvements in its vehicle deliveries, pre-tax adjusted earnings and capital expenditures.
The new guidance calls for a pre-tax adjusted loss of between $1.75 billion and $1.85 billion — a $100 million improvement at the midpoint from its prior guidance — vehicle deliveries of between 67,000 and 70,000 units, up from at least 65,000; and capital expenditures of between $1.4 billion and $1.5 billion, $300 million less at the midpoint.
Rivian attributed the improvement in its pre-tax adjusted earnings guidance to better-than-expected revenue related to its sales of regulatory credits, an IEEPA tariff refund receivable in the third quarter and its expected increase in vehicle deliveries.
The R2 — the first deliveries of which arrived to customers in June — has become Rivian's best-selling model and was responsible for "much of the gain quarter-over-quarter," the company said.
Rivian delivered a record 19,248 units from July through September. The company does not disclose deliveries by vehicle.
The EV maker remains unprofitable overall but continued to narrow its losses during the quarter. The company reported a net loss attributable to common stockholders of $913 million, compared with a loss of $1.17 billion during the third quarter of 2025.
Rivian's gross profit, which is closely monitored by investors, was $176 million during the third quarter, up from $24 million a year earlier. Its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was a loss of $435 million, a $167 million improvement from the same period last year.
The company reported that its software and services segment continues to grow, generating $605 million in revenue and a gross profit of $256 million, a 42% margin. That compares to its automotive operations, which recorded nearly $1.55 billion in revenue and a gross loss of $80 million.
Also on Thursday, Rivian reiterated that it expects the R2, a smaller and less expensive sibling to its current luxury R1S SUV, to have a positive gross margin by the end of the year. CEO RJ Scaringe has said the company needs to scale beyond current R2 production plans of 160,000 units in order to achieve overall profitability.
"That ramp-up is critical for us getting to positive gross margin on R2 and that ultimately will contribute to positive gross margin for the business," Scaringe told CNBC's Phil LeBeau during an interview Thursday. "We're going to see that through the end of the quarter and the unit economics will continue to grow … into Q1 of next year as well."
Rivian on Thursday said its cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments balance was $5.5 billion, up from $5.3 billion to end the second quarter.

articles.title_orig: Opinion | Can Canada, UK and Australia grasp chance offered by US-China rivalry?
articles.title_zh: Opinion | Can Canada, UK and Australia grasp chance offered by US-China rivalry?
articles.content_orig:
As the US shifts away from its commitment to global primacy, these Anglosphere nations have the potential to be a pivotal force for global stability
As middle powers, Australia, Britain and Canada can do more than most other nations to influence global peace in the face of a new great power rivalry between China and the United States. These three nations owe their citizens, and perhaps the wider world, an earnest effort to rise to the challenge of being peacemakers.
They have three attributes in common that give them unique potential to be a pivotal force. First is their own shared histories as members of the Anglosphere and therefore close allies of the US. Second is the recent US impetuousness and erratic behaviour towards the three of them, which demands greater independence and balance in their international relationships. Third is their shared middle power status, affording them enough diplomatic, military and trade significance to have great influence.
Today, though, Australia’s, Britain’s and Canada’s results as agents for global stability are mixed.

articles.title_orig: Hackers Swipe Millions From Polymarket Users in Latest Security Breach
articles.title_zh: Hackers Swipe Millions From Polymarket Users in Latest Security Breach
articles.content_orig:
Security incident linked to performance-monitoring tool spurred platform to halt trading for about an hour
Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international platform on Thursday because of a security incident that compromised a third-party provider, the company said.
Trading was paused for about an hour and resumed on Thursday afternoon. The company has promised to fully reimburse any affected traders.
The prediction market platform said it halted trading “out of an abundance of caution” after identifying and fixing the issue affecting its international platform.
“We’ll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders,” the company posted on X once trading had resumed.
Polymarket said it referred the incident to a law enforcement agency in the United Kingdom.
Reports have linked the source of the incident to DebugBear, a UK-based company offering website performance-monitoring tools.
DebugBear’s own website was unavailable on Thursday afternoon and the company posted on X that it was “impacted by an ongoing security incident”. It also advised clients who were using one of its products to remove the embed code from their websites. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
It was not immediately clear to what extent traders using the popular prediction market platform were affected, or the breadth of the impact. The company said anyone who was affected “will be made whole”.

articles.title_orig: Subcutaneous Toripalimab Plus Disitamab Vedotin sNDA Is Accepted in China for HER2-Expressing Urothelial Cancer
articles.title_zh: Subcutaneous Toripalimab Plus Disitamab Vedotin sNDA Is Accepted in China for HER2-Expressing Urothelial Cancer
articles.content_orig:
China's National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) has accepted a supplemental new drug application seeking the approval of a subcutaneous formulation of toripalimab (Loqtorzi; JS001sc) in combination with disitamab vedotin (Aidixi) as first-line treatment for patients with HER2-expressing locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma. 1 The application covers tumors with a HER2 immunohistochemistry score of 1+, 2+, or 3+.
With this filing, the NMPA has now accepted applications for subcutaneous toripalimab across all 13 indications for which intravenous toripalimab is approved in China. The agency accepted applications for 12 of those indications in March 2026, making JS001sc the first domestically developed subcutaneous anti–PD-1 monoclonal antibody in China to reach the new drug application stage.
In May 2026, the NMPA approved intravenous toripalimab plus disitamab vedotin for first-line treatment of HER2-expressing locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma, marking the 13th approved indication for toripalimab in mainland China. 2 Toripalimab had previously been approved in China in 2021 for advanced urothelial carcinoma in the second line or later.
The regulatory decision for the frontline combination was based on findings from the phase 3 RC48-C016 trial (NCT05302284), which enrolled patients at 74 centers across China.
RC48-C016 was a multicenter, open-label, randomized phase 3 trial in which 484 patients with previously untreated HER2-expressing locally advanced or metastatic urothelial cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to disitamab vedotin plus toripalimab every 2 weeks or gemcitabine plus cisplatin or carboplatin every 3 weeks. 3
Progression-free survival (PFS) by blinded independent review and overall survival (OS) served as dual primary end points, and secondary end points included objective response and safety.
At a median follow-up of 18.2 months, the median PFS was 13.1 months with the combination vs 6.5 months with chemotherapy (HR, 0.36; 95% CI, 0.28-0.46; P < .001). Additionally, the respective median OS values were 31.5 vs 16.9 months  (HR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.41-0.73; P < .001). The objective response rate (ORR) was 76.1% (95% CI, 70.3%-81.3%) vs 50.2% (95% CI, 43.7%-56.7%).
Median duration of response was 14.6 months with the combination vs 5.6 months with chemotherapy. 2
Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse effects (AEs) occurred in 55.1% of patients in the combination arm and 86.9% of those in the chemotherapy arm. 3
Toripalimab is an anti–PD-1 monoclonal antibody that blocks the interaction between PD-1 and its ligands, PD-L1 and PD-L2, and also induces internalization of the PD-1 receptor. Disrupting this signaling helps restore the immune system’s ability to recognize and attack tumor cells. 2
Disitamab vedotin is a HER2-directed antibody-drug conjugate composed of a humanized antibody, a protease-cleavable linker, and the cytotoxic payload monomethyl auristatin E. After binding to HER2 and being internalized by tumor cells, the conjugate releases its microtubule-disrupting payload. The combination therefore pairs targeted cytotoxic delivery with immune checkpoint inhibition.
Evidence for subcutaneous toripalimab has been derived from the phase 3 JS001sc-002-III-NSCLC study (NCT06505837), which compared subcutaneous with intravenous toripalimab, each given with chemotherapy, in patients with recurrent or metastatic nonsquamous non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). 1 The study met its primary end point in November 2025. In an oral presentation at the 2026 European Lung Cancer Congress, investigators reported that toripalimab exposure with the subcutaneous formulation was noninferior to that of the intravenous version, with similar efficacy and safety.
JS001sc-002-III-NSCLC is an open-label, randomized, multicenter phase 3 trial comparing the pharmacokinetics, efficacy, and safety of subcutaneous and intravenous toripalimab, each combined with chemotherapy, as first-line therapy for recurrent or metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC. 4
Patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to subcutaneous toripalimab 360 mg or intravenous toripalimab 240 mg, each given every 3 weeks, along with pemetrexed and cisplatin or carboplatin for 4 cycles. Those whose disease had not progressed then received maintenance pemetrexed with their assigned toripalimab formulation, with total toripalimab treatment capped at 35 cycles.
The study’s primary end points were the observed serum trough concentration at the end of cycle 1 and the model-predicted area under the concentration-time curve from day 0 to day 21 of cycle 1. Secondary end points included ORR, PFS, 6-month PFS rate, disease control rate, duration of response, and safety, which was assessed through AEs and abnormal laboratory parameters.

articles.title_orig: Audio recordings reveal decisions made moments before deadly train crash in Spain
articles.title_zh: Audio recordings reveal decisions made moments before deadly train crash in Spain
articles.content_orig:
New audio obtained by Spanish media reveals that the operator of a stopped train called a control center to say she could not restart the train as another behind it sped ahead in its direction. The resulting crash of the two high-speed trains Wednesday killed at least 69 people and injured dozens more. As of Thursday, 67 passengers remained missing, according to Spanish officials.
Many questions remain about the failures that led to one of Spain’s worst transportation disasters in decades and whether something could have been done to prevent it. Audio recordings of communications between the train operators and staff members at a control center in Madrid shed light on the decisions made in the minutes before the trains collided.
Spain’s transportation minister, Óscar Puente, said Wednesday that a security system stopped working because of a computer malfunction, causing multiple trains on the line to stop at about 8:30 a.m. local time. With the computer system down, rail traffic was then handed over to the control center in Madrid.
At about 8:36 a.m., the control center authorized a state-owned Renfe high-speed train to resume its journey, without speed limitations, even though a stationary ‌train from the private rail company Iryo was on the tracks ahead, Puente said. An erroneous ​decision was ‌made ⁠to restart the ⁠Renfe train, breaking protocol, he said.
Audio obtained by Spanish media of the conversations between the operators of both trains and the control center sheds light on the series of decisions leading up to the collision at about 8:53 a.m., near the train station in Urda. NBC News has not been able to independently verify the authenticity of the audio.
After the computer system went down, the control center told the Renfe train operator to resume its journey “at normal speed,” according to an audio clip.
“At normal speed? OK,” the operator responded.
“OK, we’ll talk later,” the controller said before signing off.
Several minutes later, someone from the control center called the Iryo train to authorize it to also continue on its normal journey, according to an audio clip.
The operator of the Iryo train, which was ahead of the Renfe train, called back seven minutes later to say she had been unable to restart it. “I’m still stopped at the entrance signal,” she said, according to the audio clip. The control center told her to restart the train when she could and to call back if she had further problems, according to the audio. Several minutes later, the Renfe train ran into the back of the Iryo train.
The crash, the second deadly high-speed rail train collision this year in Spain, sent shock waves across the country. Until recently, the high-speed rail network was considered one of Spain’s crowning achievements. The crash came just weeks ahead of a major election in Spain, and it has led to criticism of the government and protests.
In January, a separate disaster on the same rail line killed 46 people. Several days later, a commuter train near Barcelona derailed, killing the driver and injuring dozens of other people.
Hundreds of emergency workers, firefighters, police officers and soldiers responded to the scene of Wednesday’s crash to rescue survivors and recover bodies. Cranes were brought in to move parts of the damaged trains later in the day.
Spain has the largest high-speed rail network in Europe for trains moving at more than 155 mph, with more than 1,900 miles of track, according to the European Union.
The identities of victims have begun to emerge.
Fátima Báñez, a former minister, was among those killed in the collision, according to the leader of Spain’s opposition Popular Party.
“She was a tireless woman, a loyal friend, and always committed to improving the lives of Spaniards,” Alberto Núñez Feijóo wrote in Spanish on social media .
Antonio Acedo, the driver of one of the trains, was also killed, according to the Izquierda Española political party.
“Antonio was an exceptional person, a kind, prudent, and dedicated man,” the party wrote on social media .
The country is observing three days of mourning after the crash.
Dirk Llorens, an American who lives in Madrid, said he and his wife were on the stopped train when, suddenly, “I was thrown just violently, just over my table.”
“Then the train started sliding, and I could see that the roof had opened, and there was dust flying out of the back,” he said.
People were panicking and did not know what had just happened, he said. Llorens thought the train had derailed somehow. He turned and saw that “everything was destroyed.”
Llorens said that as he and his wife tried to escape from the train, he saw people who had “smashed their face” during the impact, with bloody noses and cuts on their heads spewing blood.
He said that the crash occurred on a hill and that “we were all just trying to get out because we thought the train would roll on the hill and kill us.”
As more injured people escaped from the train, Llorens saw a man “come out completely full of blood, and he was just sitting on a tree, just completely collapsed.”
“I think people were so in shock. We were all in shock,” he said.
Those who were less injured began trying to help one another, he said, adding that soon afterward, a large group of paramedics and police arrived.
“You really never know what can happen in life — that makes you appreciate life but also understand that some things can happen at any time,” Llorens said.
He called for transparency from the Spanish government about what happened.
“The Spanish government really needs to put all their effort in making sure that something like that doesn’t ever happen again,” he said. “I don’t think I’ll take a train in Spain unless I see that they’re having big improvements in what they’re doing.”
Daniella Silva is a national reporter for NBC News, focusing on immigration.
Hernan Muñoz is a freelancer based in Spain.

articles.title_orig: EU seeks 'highest level' ties with Canada in Montreal summit
articles.title_zh: EU seeks 'highest level' ties with Canada in Montreal summit
articles.content_orig:
European Union and Canadian leaders are set to meet at a special Canada-EU summit to discuss critical policies like artificial inteligence (AI), climate, energy and ⁠security.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Thursday, ahead of the summit, which begins on Friday, that the EU will continue to explore Canada's prospects for becoming the bloc's first "associate member."
But despite her comments, the summit's declaration is expected to exclude the term "associate member," a move pushed by Germany and other members.
"Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession," Von der Leyen clarified. "We can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before."
"We both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible," von der Leyen added.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had said this week he wasn't concerned about the  "associate member" status, or "specific names" to be given to the new alliance with the EU .
"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians," Carney added.
Ottawa's quest for deeper ties to Europe is seen as a move to reduce its reliance on the US since President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a range of Canadian goods .
Frederic Merand, political expert on EU-Canada relations at the University of Montreal, spoke to DW about how the summit serves as "political impetus" to improve the bilateral trade relationship and to free Canada of its reliance on the US.
"It's not going to happen, over time, overnight. And every time we move closer to the Europeans, we realize how dependent we are on the US and how also vulnerable we are to, for example, us retaliation," Merand said.
But he added that courting the EU is also part of a broader strategy "to reinvent the Canadian economy, to create a single market, to attract more investment," as well as to diversify our partnerships with China, India and also other parts of the world.
The EU is "a natural partner" to work with, Merand said, given its existing free trade agreement with Canada, in addition to the close historical and cultural ties between the two partners.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
An EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that Canada and the EU sought to align policies in areas such as climate, energy and artificial intelligence, allowing Ottawa to participate in some EU programs.
Canada has critical minerals needed for green technologies such as batteries and wind turbines, something for which Europe normally relies on China.
But Canada is in need of major infrastructure investment to develop its mining industry.
There are hopes that the summit can result in a plan for the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects.
EU and Canadian leaders are also looking into a digital trade deal that can allow for faster and cheaper online transactions.
Additionally, Canada could be allowed to participate in the EU's Erasmus youth program, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad.

articles.title_orig: Israel election result shows no overall majority as vote count complete
articles.title_zh: Israel election result shows no overall majority as vote count complete
articles.content_orig:
Vote counting is complete in Israel’s elections with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition winning a majority in parliament, Israeli media have said.
As the provisional results were being published on Thursday, opposition politicians met to explore options for a coalition.
With more than 99 percent of Tuesday’s ballots tallied, Netanyahu’s bloc held 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot secured 48 seats, Israeli outlet Haaretz reported. The Arab list parties, meanwhile, held a combined 19 seats, it added.
Both Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition parties fell short of securing the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority.
The final results of the Knesset elections will be certified and announced by Wednesday. Until that date, the results are subject to change.
Tuesday’s elections – the first since the October 7, 2023, attacks on southern Israel and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza – were widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s premiership.
On Thursday, Eisenkot, who heads the Yashar party, met former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together party, to discuss ways to form a new government “as quickly as possible”, according to a statement reported by Israel’s Ynet News outlet.
Eisenkot also met Democrats party chairman Yair Golan, the only member of the opposition alliance to support forming a coalition with parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, while all other political groups have rejected any such union.
Golan met separately with Mansour Abbas, who leads the United Arab list, or Ra’am, which is projected to win seven of the 19 Arab party seats.
“This is a time for action. Our responsibility is not to miss the opportunity for change and the salvation of Israel,” Golan said in a post on X after his meeting with Abbas.
Al Jazeera correspondent Nour Odeh noted that “Eisenkot has an uphill battle ahead of him.”
The former military leader-turned-politician has pledged “not to ally himself or get into a partnership with the Palestinian Israeli parties”, Odeh said, reporting from the occupied West Bank because Al Jazeera is banned from Israel.
But given the fact that no political bloc has a majority, the Eisenkot-led opposition bloc cannot form a governing coalition without the support of Arab-led parties, she added.
Meanwhile, Netanyahu’s Likud party has continued to amplify unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance – claims that have been rejected .
The head of the Central Elections Committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought to him in a letter to the Shin Bet security agency. Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims, but given their serious nature, he asked the agency to investigate.
Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of working to delegitimise the election results with his allegations.
In a video posted on his X account, Eisenkot said: “The days of Netanyahu using state institutions against Israeli interests for his personal needs are over,” adding that no “spin” can change voters rejecting his government at the polls.
“Benjamin Netanyahu is not satisfied with the results, no matter how much he has been saying that he won,” political analyst Xavier Abu Eid told Al Jazeera.
He added that while it seems unlikely the opposition could take advantage by overcoming differences with the Arab-led groups, there could be an understanding to replace the current speaker of the Knesset, who is close to Netanyahu.
“If there is a new speaker in the Knesset, … Netanyahu loses an important ally,” Abu Eid said, adding that this might give an opening for the opposition to “actually start passing legislation” against him.
Odeh said the next steps would involve negotiations between political groups after the Central Elections Committee announces and certifies the election results by Wednesday.
